**Case and dockets:** Almendarez-Torres v. United States, No. 96-6839.
**Event and date:** Merits decision, 1998-03-24; October Term 1997, chunk 6.
**Result:** Reversed and remanded, 5–4; enhanced sentence vacated; resentencing on the existing charge capped at §1326(a)’s maximum.
**Version / lineage:** Original decision; durable Record integrated into the current-term workspace. No repository commit is asserted.

## Event, posture and law entering decision

Research cutoff: 1998-03-24. The frozen neutral packet supplies the argument date, review channel under 28 U.S.C. §1254(1), charged omission, plea admission, preserved objection and sentence. All nine sitting Justices participate at both milestones; quorum is present and five votes decide. The source does not establish the exact found-in date, and no unsupported temporal issue is adjudicated. No post-event authority is used.

The relevant entering law is the complete Custis, Watts/Putra, Gaudin and Old Chief entries in [the authorized slice](../entering-law/OT_1997CHUNK6_A.md), together with the [validated neutral packet](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK6_A_VALIDATED_NEUTRAL.md). Rogers supplies no admission exception or harmless-error holding. The prepared law remains valid through this event; no intervening decision changes the charge/classification question. The facts extracted from the historical report remain facts at the published-recitation level, not new findings.

## Stone's approved core and final compatibility

The complete [approved supplement](../runtime/CHUNK6_SCOPED/almendarez_torres_v_united_states_STONE.md) directs reversal, vacatur of the enhanced sentence and resentencing within subsection (a) on this charge. Stone expressly reaches constitutional allocation and adopts the element construction because the prior conviction changes the authorized maximum. His Part I join adopts precisely that statutory rule, its charge/proof consequence and remedy, not the four Associates' decision to stop at constitutional doubt. His concurrence preserves the definitive constitutional ground and all approved exclusions. There is no substantive narrowing, imported discretion, or standing-fallback use. The existing law reserves the constitutional issue and does not contradict his approved proposal.

## Opinion form and judgment before assignment

One signed plenary lead opinion is appropriate because one statutory classification resolves one sentence judgment. Its common statutory-rule and remedy part has five direct joins; its avoidance explanation has only four. The separate concurrence performs the necessary work of preserving Stone's different constitutional ground. A four-Justice dissent preserves the competing penalty construction. These parts follow the actual legal disagreement; they are not divided to manipulate eligibility or counts. No Marks synthesis is necessary for the expressly shared statutory rule, and no constitutional majority is manufactured.

## Controlling law of the decision

### Section 1326(b)(2) requires an aggravated-offense allegation before its higher maximum may apply

**Holding and operative rule:** The prior aggravated-felony conviction specified in §1326(b)(2) is an element of the aggravated unlawful-reentry offense. It must be alleged in the federal indictment and, unless validly admitted as an element of the charged offense, proved to the jury beyond a reasonable doubt; an admission to the fact of a prior conviction does not cure its omission from this indictment, so the existing conviction permits no sentence above §1326(a)'s two-year maximum.

**Authority:** Part I of Scalia's opinion is joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter and Ginsburg. These five expressly adopt the statutory rule, its ordinary element consequences and the remedy. Four explain the construction through constitutional avoidance; Stone-Zsela gives a definitive constitutional ground separately. No majority adopts a general constitutional rule governing all facts that increase a statutory maximum.

**Controlling explanation:** The Court holds that subsection (a)'s complete unlawful-reentry offense and two-year maximum must be distinguished from subsection (b)(2)'s aggravated offense carrying a twenty-year maximum. The prior conviction authorizes a different punishment ceiling; it does more than inform selection of punishment within the ordinary range. The provisions' cross-references permit that element construction. Hamling requires the indictment to state the offense's elements, and Gaudin requires proof of an actual element to the jury beyond a reasonable doubt when it has not validly been admitted. Almendarez-Torres admitted the prior convictions, but the indictment did not charge that aggravating element. His factual admission therefore does not answer the preserved objection to the punishment legally authorized by this charge.

The traditional use of recidivism at sentencing does not decide this statute's classification. McMillan addressed a minimum within an unchanged maximum, and Watts permits ordinary sentencing findings within conviction-based authority while reserving element evasion and other constitutional limits. Custis addresses collateral attacks on existing convictions, not the indictment's content. Old Chief confirms that prior-conviction status can be proved without unnecessary prejudicial detail; that evidentiary concern does not require treating status as a sentencing factor. The decision does not determine a subsidiary standard-of-proof claim, invalidate the admitted prior convictions, select a replacement sentence, or decide facts that do not increase the statutory maximum.

**Precedent treatment:** Hamling and Gaudin govern the consequences of the statutory classification; McMillan, Watts, Custis and Old Chief retain the distinct boundaries stated below.

## Adaptive audit annex

### Frozen commitments and historical reconciliation

The following immutable reconciliation is incorporated verbatim for the eight Associate commitments, grounds, join limits and historical comparison:

## Almendarez-Torres v. United States — No. 96-6839 — March 24, 1998

### Reconciled rules and judgment components

**P — penalty construction and bounded constitutional conclusion:** Section 1326(b)(2) authorizes enhanced punishment for the alien described in subsection (a) whose deportation followed an aggravated-felony conviction; it does not create an additional offense requiring that prior conviction to be charged in this indictment. Congress may make that prior-adjudication, recidivist status a sentencing factor in this setting. The reciprocal cross-references, recidivist subject and punishment structure provide the statutory ground. McMillan's unchanged-maximum setting and Watts's ordinary sentencing holding do not by themselves resolve this maximum increase; the distinct recidivism basis must do that work. Affirm the Fifth Circuit's sentence judgment.

**E — statutory element construction through constitutional avoidance:** The statute fairly permits treating the prior aggravated-felony conviction as the element authorizing the higher range. The increase from the ordinary two-year maximum to twenty years creates serious constitutional doubt, and the available element construction avoids deciding the constitutional boundary. Hamling then requires the omitted allegation in the indictment. Set aside the sentence affirmance and remand for lawful sentencing on the charged offense. This does not decide that every maximum-increasing fact, or every recidivist provision, must constitutionally be an element.

| Justice | Final threshold, statutory/constitutional commitment and disposition | Individual reconciliation basis |
|---|---|---|
| Stevens | Reach; **E**; reverse the sentence affirmance and remand. | His McMillan dissent and public Watts dissent distinguish mandatory punitive authorization from merely receiving information. His historical join in the avoidance dissent, 523 U.S. 248–271, rests on the same open maximum-allocation question and available construction. His broader proof concerns need not become the common ground. |
| O'Connor | Reach; **P**; affirm. | Her McMillan majority join and Custis opinion permit genuine sentencing allocation while retaining constitutional limits. Her historical penalty/recidivism join, 523 U.S. 228–248, has no displaced premise: current Watts did not resolve this classification. |
| Scalia | Reach; **E**; reverse and remand on the statutory ground. | His Gaudin opinion and bounded Watts join require protection of actual elements without settling every sentencing fact. The full historical dissent expressly declines the definitive constitutional answer, including at 260; its footnotes and conclusion support avoidance, not a universal constitutional rule. The same objection remains. |
| Kennedy | Reach; **P**; affirm. | His Custis and Witte joins support treating existing conviction status distinctly. His Watts dissent sought plenary process, now supplied, rather than a merits prohibition. The historical P join supplies strong evidence with no concrete altered premise. |
| Souter | Reach; **E**; reverse and remand. | His Gaudin, Old Chief and bounded Watts positions preserve actual-element protections and the difference between range selection and authority to enlarge the ceiling. His historical avoidance join remains compatible with each. No categorical sentencing theory is added. |
| Thomas | Reach; **P**; affirm. | His Custis, Gaudin and Watts joins distinguish prior status, actual elements and ordinary sentencing without predeciding classification. His historical P join confirms the specific textual recidivism conclusion; no later-career position is used. |
| Ginsburg | Reach; **E**; reverse and remand. | Her Old Chief opinion preserves the status element while controlling prejudicial proof; Custis concerns collateral review. The historical dissent's treatment of prejudice and indictment, including 268–269, remains available and supports her frozen E commitment. |
| Breyer | Reach; **P**; affirm. | His Witte and Watts joins and Watts policy concurrence distinguish constitutional permission from preferred sentencing policy. The historical recidivism ground answers the ceiling difference without converting Watts into an unlimited safe harbor. |

**Proposition coalitions:** O'Connor, Kennedy, Thomas and Breyer join P at the stated statutory and constitutional levels. Stevens, Scalia, Souter and Ginsburg join E at the statutory-avoidance level. Agreement in E does not decide the ultimate constitutional question, and no additional separate writing is needed merely to restate Stevens's broader concerns.

**Historical comparison and limits:** All eight Associate positions match the historical disposition and operative grounds. The present Gaudin/Watts/Old Chief formulations sharpen boundaries already left open; they do not supply a concrete changed premise for any different Associate vote. The original 1988 aggravated maximum was fifteen years; the applicable copied 1994 text supplies twenty. The plea admission is not an intentional waiver of the preserved indictment objection. On P, the admission reinforces the bounded application but does not substitute for classification. The petitioner presented no separate subsidiary proof-burden claim; heightened proof for unusually consequential sentencing findings remains undecided. On E, the basic guilty plea is not automatically withdrawn, no acquittal is entered and no replacement term is selected. Missing original indictment or plea materials establish no default.

### Final joins, assignment and count receipt

The final judgment coalition is Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Scalia, Souter and Ginsburg. Stone joins Part I only; the four Associates join both lead parts. O'Connor, Kennedy, Thomas and Breyer reject both lead parts and join the dissent. No conditional commitment is enlarged; the constitutional disagreement remains publicly visible. The necessary common statutory proposition is directly supported by five, while the avoidance explanation is noncontrolling as an explanation of constitutional scope.

Chief Justice Stone-Zsela assigns. Counts freshly recomputed from the actual opinion tables copied in [the baseline](../runtime/OT_1997CHUNK6_ASSIGNMENT_BASELINE.md): **Stone-Zsela 4; Stevens 5; O'Connor 6; Scalia 5; Kennedy 6; Souter 6; Thomas 5; Ginsburg 6; Breyer 6**. Total: 49. Last counted event: United States v. Robinson, March 23, 1998, Kennedy. The [recount receipt](../runtime/OT_1997CHUNK6_A_ASSEMBLY_RECOUNT.json) records the individual source authors, not prior tallies.

Eligible authors for the complete lead are Stevens, Scalia, Souter and Ginsburg; each joins both the common statutory part and the avoidance explanation. Stone's partial join does not qualify for the complete lead. Minimum eligible count: 5; balance pool: Stevens (5), Scalia (5), Souter (6) and Ginsburg (6). Scalia is selected. His Gaudin analysis of the actual element/jury boundary and his frozen insistence on resolving this case through an available statutory construction fit the necessary separation between classification and a constitutional question left undecided by the four. Stevens is the strongest lower-count alternative, but his broader proof concerns supply no additional accommodation needed here. The common formulation already preserves each necessary commitment; this is fit, not expansion based merely on a close vote. O'Connor writes the dissent because her Custis treatment of existing-conviction status directly fits its recidivist distinction; this separate writing does not count. The lead adds one Scalia count.

**Historical departure:** The Court reverses rather than historically affirming because Stone replaces the historical Chief's penalty-construction vote with his approved element construction and constitutional ground. The four Associates supporting reversal retain their historical avoidance positions, and the four supporting affirmance retain their historical recidivism positions; no Associate departure or new constitutional join is attributed to them.

### Validation record

The five-to-four judgment, five-Justice Part I, four-Justice Part II and four-Justice dissent reconcile. Stone's concurrence supplies no extra vote beyond his Part I and judgment vote. The common rule has a direct majority; neither constitutional explanation does. The controlling explanation is below 350 words. The source cutoff, natural key, complete mandate and eleven Public Projection blocks are present. No modern provenance enters the Public Projection.

## Continuity and validation status

The Opinion Topology and Separate Writings below preserve every published material position for continuity at its stated scope; noncontrolling positions create no current law. The Procedure After Action block specifies the actual remaining stage. Final compatibility was tested against all eight frozen commitments and Stone’s complete approved supplement. No material Associate commitment changes at assembly, and no invented circulation exchange supplies a join. The form, tally, exact joins, remedy and authority distinctions are checked locally. assignment_statements.text:
**Case and dockets:** Ohio Adult Parole Authority v. Woodard, No. 96-1769.
**Event and date:** Merits decision, 1998-03-25; October Term 1997, chunk 6.
**Result:** Due-process remand reversed, 8–1; self-incrimination remand reversed, 9–0; independent no-entitlement ruling undisturbed.
**Version / lineage:** Original decision; durable Record integrated into the current-term workspace. No repository commit is asserted.

## Event, source boundary and law entering decision

Research cutoff: 1998-03-25. Certiorari jurisdiction under §1254(1), nine participants at argument and decision, quorum present, ordinary five-Justice threshold. The frozen neutral Woodard section supplies the complete material posture and the pleaded restrictions; the [Woodard reconciliation](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK6_WOODARD_RECONCILED.md) controls all Associate commitments. The [entering-law slice](../entering-law/OT_1997CHUNK6_A.md), [Johnson public projection](../entering-law/chunk6_a_sources/current_johnson_v_rodriguez_public.md), and LaChance appendix supply actual current law. Almendarez-Torres's March 24 classification rule changes no clemency or privilege predicate here.

The original filings were not independently recovered; the source recitations support the specified allegations and lower judgments. No fabricated process opportunity, waiver, silence penalty or actual use of statements enters the decision. Historical Sandin's hardship test is not current governing law. The present event is merits review of two §1983 claims, not a covered emergency application.

## Stone's fixed core and joins

The [complete approved supplement](../runtime/CHUNK6_SCOPED/ohio_adult_parole_authority_v_woodard_STONE.md) directs reversal on both presented claims, identifies discretionary executive clemency as distinct from another criminal trial and judicial collateral review, preserves a minimal safeguard against fundamentally arbitrary procedure, and finds no compelled self-incrimination from this voluntary interview. The exact joins below implement those propositions. The broader appellate-analogy discussion and hypothetical civil-inference alternative are additional Associate grounds; neither is attributed to Stone. He joins the no-right-to-clemency conclusion, the trial/mercy distinction, both Part II holdings and Part III-A. No new remedy, no narrowing to access alone and no standing-fallback use is necessary. His public grounds are fully represented in those joins, so a redundant separate writing is unnecessary.

## Form-first determination

One signed lead opinion addresses two independent constitutional claims, with the actual due-process divisions and the distinct self-incrimination alternative identified in parts. The minimum-process rule has six direct joins and its application five. A Kennedy concurrence preserves three Associates' different process ground; a Stevens partial dissent preserves his further-process position. No part is created or divided to affect assignment counts. O'Connor, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer can each carry the complete lead, so divided authorship is unnecessary.

## Controlling law of the decision

### I. Required clemency procedures do not create an entitlement to mercy or triallike review

**Holding and operative rule:** Ohio's required investigation, hearing and advisory recommendation do not create a substantive entitlement to clemency because they do not constrain the Governor to grant it on specified facts. The analogy to a first appeal as of right does not itself require appellate representation, triallike evidence procedure or a new determination of guilt in this discretionary executive process.

**Authority:** Part I-A has all eight Associates, with Stone-Zsela also joining the no-right-to-mercy conclusion. Part I-B has O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer; Stone-Zsela joins only the mercy-versus-criminal-trial distinction. Stevens does not join the rejection of the established-process analogy.

**Controlling explanation:** Dumschat distinguishes seeking clemency from entitlement to its grant. Sandin requires a genuine substantive constraint on a meaningful deprivation; Doe and Johnson likewise distinguish required administration from an entitlement to a favorable discretionary decision. Ohio must investigate, hold the required hearing and recommend action even after an execution stay, but its recommendation is advisory and the Governor retains complete discretion. A later hearing or revised recommendation on new information is permitted, not required. These provisions do not compel clemency.

Evitts protects the first appeal as of right within adjudication of guilt. Clemency performs a different executive function. Its availability after conviction does not itself import appellate or trial procedure. The Court rejects the Sixth Circuit's general integral-stage theory as a basis for the requested remand, while preserving independently retained constitutional rights. Herrera's record-specific innocence ruling establishes no rule that executive mercy is the exclusive constitutionally sufficient substitute for every claim of innocence.

### II. Capital-clemency procedures retain a constitutional minimum, satisfied on these pleadings

**Holding and operative rule:** An established capital-clemency process must afford minimal safeguards against fundamentally arbitrary procedure, including arbitrary denial of any access or substitution of an entirely arbitrary device such as a coin flip for consideration. The notice and offered interview here, considered with the pleaded restrictions, satisfy that minimum; they establish no entitlement to clemency, trial protections, a favorable recommendation or judicial review of mercy's merits.

**Authority:** Part II-A's minimum safeguard has six direct joins: O'Connor, Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer. Part II-B's sufficient-process application has five: O'Connor, Stone-Zsela, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer. Stevens disputes the application; Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas agree with rejection of the claim on their distinct entitlement/adjudication ground. Both controlling propositions rest on direct majority joins, without combining separate rationales under Marks.

**Controlling explanation:** A valid death sentence reduces the process owed before discretionary mercy is denied, but the prisoner remains alive. That retained interest supplies a minimum protection independent of a state-created entitlement to release. Ford illustrates the distinction between the interest protected and the flexible procedure appropriate to it; this case does not import Ford's separate prohibition on executing an incompetent prisoner or its particular hearing requirements.

Woodard alleges three days' interview notice, ten days' hearing notice, difficulty preparing while postconviction proceedings continued, exclusion of counsel from the interview, chair-controlled counsel participation at the hearing, and inability to testify or submit documents at the hearing. Accepting that pleaded account, the notice and offered personal interview provided access, and those restrictions do not establish fundamentally arbitrary procedure requiring further adjudication. The Court does not find an unmentioned alternative document channel or reject the allegations as untrue. It establishes neither a fixed list of required safeguards nor an accuracy code for every disputed item in a clemency file. Johnson's rejection of a parole-file process entitlement does not extinguish independent constitutional protection.

### III. The optional interview does not establish compelled self-incrimination

**Holding and operative rule:** An optional clemency interview does not compel self-incrimination merely because the prisoner must choose between providing potentially harmful information and remaining silent; absence of counsel, confidentiality or immunity does not itself convert this invitation into compulsion. The conclusion also holds if an ordinary civil adverse inference from silence is assumed, but it does not authorize an automatic privilege penalty, compelled waiver or criminal use of compelled answers.

**Authority:** Part III-A's present voluntary-interview holding has all nine Justices. Part III-B's additional ordinary-inference ground and its limits have all eight Associates; Stone-Zsela does not join that additional ground.

**Controlling explanation:** Murphy distinguishes a difficult evidentiary choice from a command backed by a genuine threatened penalty for asserting the privilege. Woodard was invited, not required, to attend or answer. The State's refusal to promise confidentiality or immunity does not establish that it compelled answers. No automatic loss of clemency eligibility for silence, compelled waiver or criminal use of compelled testimony is established.

The eight Associates additionally apply Baxter's distinction between ordinary adverse inferences in civil proceedings and automatic sanctions attached to silence. Even assuming such an inference in this civil clemency evaluation, the voluntary choice does not become compelled testimony. The record does not establish Ohio's actual use of silence or answers; the assumption supplies an alternative legal ground, not a factual finding. LaChance preserves separately supported compulsion and waiver claims, and Johnson confirms that absence of entitlement to a benefit does not excuse an independent unconstitutional penalty. A materially supported coercive condition would therefore require its own analysis.

## Adaptive audit annex

### Frozen commitments and reconciliation

The following operative propositions, eight-Justice table and historical-premise audit are copied from the immutable reconciliation:

## Reconciled operative propositions

**A — no state-created entitlement.** Ohio's mandatory investigation, hearing and advisory recommendation do not meaningfully constrain the Governor to grant clemency on specified substantive facts. They therefore create neither a right to mercy nor the claimed full adjudicatory procedure. Dumschat distinguishes seeking clemency from being entitled to receive it; the actual Sandin rule, Doe's procedure/substance distinction and Johnson's initial-parole holding reinforce that boundary. Mandatory procedures alone are insufficient. The lack of such an entitlement does not extinguish independently retained constitutional rights.

**B — the appellate analogy does not itself require the requested procedures.** First appeal as of right and discretionary executive mercy perform different functions. Evitts does not require Ohio to import appellate representation, triallike evidence procedures or a new guilt adjudication into this clemency process merely because mercy follows conviction. Seven Associates reject the Sixth Circuit's general integral-stage theory as a basis for the due-process remand here. Stevens preserves the narrower established-process and retained-life analogy described below; he does not demand trial machinery or an automatic process formula based on distance from trial.

**C — minimum safeguards protecting remaining life.** A condemned prisoner remains alive and retains a constitutionally protected life interest. Although the process due after valid conviction is reduced and the ultimate mercy choice remains discretionary, some minimal procedural safeguards apply to an established capital-clemency process. Arbitrarily denying any access, or replacing consideration with an entirely arbitrary device such as a coin flip, can warrant judicial intervention. This principle creates no right to a favorable recommendation, no accuracy code for every disputed file item, no judicial reassessment of the merits of mercy and no fixed list of trial rights. Stevens, O'Connor, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer support this common proposition. Stevens's broader account of the established process and his different application remain separately identified.

**D — application and due-process remedy.** O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer would reverse the Sixth Circuit's due-process remand and sustain rejection of the present claim. O'Connor, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer apply C: the notice and offered personal interview provide access, and the particular objections do not establish failure of the minimum safeguards. Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas reach the same judgment on A and B without joining C as a general procedural-life ground. Stevens would retain a remand to examine whether the actual process affords basic fairness and meaningful participation, without finding a constitutional violation already established or prescribing each requested safeguard.

**E — voluntary interview and self-incrimination.** An optional clemency interview is not compelled self-incrimination merely because the inmate must choose between giving information that might hurt his clemency or postconviction position and remaining silent. The absence of counsel at that interview, confidentiality or immunity does not by itself compel answers. The conclusion remains true on the assumption that the Authority considers an ordinary adverse inference from silence in the civil clemency evaluation, as distinguished in Baxter from an automatic penalty for asserting the privilege. All eight Associates reject the Fifth Amendment remand on those grounds. No obligation to attend or answer, automatic ineligibility for remaining silent, compelled waiver, actual criminal use of compelled answers, or particular unlawful silence sanction is established. LaChance and Murphy preserve analysis of a materially supported compulsion or penalty; Johnson prevents treating the discretionary-benefit label as a complete defense to such a claim.

His full Murphy dissent join concerned a compulsory probation command and serious threatened sanction, not this invitation. Historical Woodard, 290–295 and all five notes, confirms the due-process remand, Evitts support and express Part III join. No current-law premise supports deleting that Evitts support or inventing a Fifth Amendment dissent. |
| O'Connor | Joins A, the limited B distinction, C and D's adequate-process application. **Reverse due-process remand.** Refuses categorical extinction of process protection. | Joins E; **reverse**. | Her Ford writing, 427–431, distinguishes the actual substantive interest from flexible minimum procedure; although its incompetency interest differs from mercy, the procedural distinction supports her historical Woodard life-interest reservation. Her Sandin dissent is not current law; she applies the actual substantive-constraint rule. Her Murphy majority join distinguishes a genuine threatened penalty from an evidentiary choice. Historical Woodard, 288–290, confirms C including the coin-flip example, D on these objections and Part III. |
| Scalia | Joins A and B and the conclusion that the pleaded procedures require no relief. Does not join C's affirmative procedural-life rule. **Reverse due-process remand.** | Joins E; **reverse**. | His Sandin dissent supplies his narrower view, but the Court's actual state-constraint rule and his full Johnson join govern. Those authorities leave Ohio's ultimate mercy discretion unconstrained. His LaChance join retains actual coercion safeguards. Historical Part II and Part III joins support the same judgments; the historical controlling-hardship premise must be replaced by actual Sandin law, as addressed below. |
| Kennedy | Joins A and B; does not join C; **reverse due-process remand**. Preserves independently grounded constitutional prohibitions. | Joins E; **reverse**. | His Johnson opinion rejects procedure-derived initial-release entitlement while preserving protection against retaliation, and his Sandin dissent does not establish current law. His LaChance join distinguishes genuine compulsion from giving voluntary information. Historical Part II/III joins remain strongly supported once the Sandin premise is corrected; no new statutory constraint or unlawful condition is shown. |

His LaChance Part IV separates actual duties, privilege and coercive use. Historical Woodard join of the O'Connor writing and Part III confirms the modest C floor, adequate-process result and noncompulsion rule, including the limited hypothetical inference. |

The table records eight commitments on each separable disposition and distinguishes the three entitlement-based procedural positions from the four minimum-process application positions. Stevens supplies a fifth supporter of C but not a fifth vote for D's application within that group. C is a directly shared proposition at its stated level, not a claim that all five join one opinion or that a Marks synthesis combines inconsistent rationales. No final Court count or author is assigned here.

## Changed entering law and historical-premise audit

The historical Part II at 283 invokes historical Sandin's atypical-and-significant-hardship formulation as an additional ground. That formulation is not the law entering this event. The current Court instead requires a genuine substantive state constraint on meaningful deprivation and leaves direct constitutional interests independent. Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas supported a hardship alternative in their earlier public Sandin dissent, but their present common state-entitlement ground cannot publish it as controlling law. Each applies the current rule to Ohio's wholly discretionary ultimate mercy choice. The required steps do not compel a favorable recommendation or grant of clemency; Dumschat and the substantive distinction made in Johnson therefore continue to support their dispositions. This is a concrete premise substitution, not a silent import of the historical Court's law or a reason to change their judgment.

**Historical departure:** Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas retain their historical rejection of the due-process claim but cannot adopt historical Woodard's reliance on a controlling Sandin hardship test: that test received only four votes in the earlier public decision, and the controlling substantive-constraint rule now governs. Their own Sandin dissent positions explain why they retain the narrower entitlement/adjudication approach, while their full joins in Johnson supply the current-law basis for finding Ohio's mandatory process insufficient to create a mercy entitlement. The altered legal premise changes that supporting authority, not their judgment or their refusal to join the affirmative retained-life floor.

The five supporters of C are not historical departures: the full O'Connor and Stevens writings already support that minimal proposition, including arbitrary consideration as well as access. Nor does recognizing C contradict Johnson: ordinary initial-parole accuracy rights are distinct from minimum safeguards for a retained life interest, and Johnson expressly reserves independent-right wrongs. This distinction explains O'Connor, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer's present adequate-process application and Stevens's remand without inventing a new state-created entitlement.

Herrera's current controlling proposition is record-specific. Neither its historical broader discussion nor the historical Woodard citation makes executive mercy an exclusive constitutionally sufficient substitute for all innocence claims. Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas may note clemency's established independent executive function, but cannot use Herrera to announce that broader rule. Stevens's life-interest and established-process position stands on his eligible Dumschat/Ford positions and the sources cited above, without depending on a historical Herrera holding absent here.

The Fifth Amendment comparison leaves no material judgment or operative-rule departure after the limited-inference clarification. The official report at 286 expressly acknowledges the missing account of actual Ohio practice and assumes adverse inferences favorably to Woodard. Baxter, 425 U.S. 316–320, distinguishes ordinary civil evidentiary inferences from automatic consequences attached to silence and compelled criminal testimony. Murphy, 465 U.S. 434–439, distinguishes a command backed by an actual or implied privilege penalty from a difficult choice. Current LaChance expressly preserves genuine compulsion and does not impose a universal ban on lawful civil inferences. Johnson addresses a different protected litigation penalty and does not turn every evidentiary disadvantage into compulsion. These actual premises support every Associate's E commitment; they do not support an unlimited rule approving punishment for silence.



### Final compatibility and assignment

No Associate changes a reconciled position. The opinion adopts C's full arbitrary-decisionmaking/access floor, preserving Stevens's Evitts disagreement and E's ordinary-inference alternative. Stone adds a sixth vote to the floor and fifth to the sufficient-process application, while the self-incrimination judgment has nine. No procedural allegation is negated and no fact beyond the neutral packet is supplied.

Stone assigns from both reversing judgment coalitions. Fresh actual-opinion-table recount, including the just-written Almendarez-Torres lead: **Stone-Zsela 4; Stevens 5; O'Connor 6; Scalia 6; Kennedy 6; Souter 6; Thomas 5; Ginsburg 6; Breyer 6**. Total counted leads: 50. Last counted event: Almendarez-Torres v. United States, March 24, 1998, Scalia. The complete-lead eligible authors are O'Connor, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer, each with 6; all four form the balance pool (minimum 6, ceiling 7). Stone does not join the complete appellate-analogy and hypothetical-inference grounds; Stevens rejects the application; Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas reject the minimum-life framework. These are substantive join limits, not capability exclusions.

O'Connor is selected for fit. Her Ford writing distinguishes the protected interest from flexible minimum procedure, the precise work necessary to explain why life remains protected without importing a trial into mercy. Souter's LaChance treatment is the strongest alternative for coordinating the compulsion issue, but that common ground is already settled; O'Connor's minimum-process formulation addresses the actual due-process boundary with no additional accommodation. This is no historical-authorship presumption. Stone is not eligible for the complete lead; his lower count cannot authorize assigning him grounds beyond his approved supplement. Kennedy's current Johnson opinion fits the concurrence's entitlement/independent-right distinction. Only O'Connor's lead adds a count.

**Historical departure:** The affirmative minimum-process proposition and its sufficient-process application now appear as direct majority holdings because Stone joins the minimum-safeguard position. Stevens retains his historical due-process remand, the four minimum-process Associates retain their historical application, and Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas retain their distinct rejection ground. Their changed Sandin supporting premise is separately explained in the incorporated reconciliation; no unsupported Associate vote change is claimed.

Due process is 8–1; privilege is 9–0. I-A has eight complete Associate joins, I-B seven, II-A six, II-B five, III-A nine and III-B eight. assignment_statements.text:
**Case and dockets:** Feltner v. Columbia Pictures Television, Inc., No. 96-1768.
**Event and date:** Merits decision, 1998-03-31; October Term 1997, chunk 6.
**Result:** Reversed and remanded, 9–0; jury determination of statutory-damages facts and amount required on the timely demand.
**Version / lineage:** Original decision; durable Record integrated into the current-term workspace. No repository commit is asserted.

## Event, entering law and source status

Research cutoff: 1998-03-31. Certiorari under §1254(1); all nine participate at argument and decision; quorum and five-vote threshold satisfied. The [validated neutral packet](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK6_A_VALIDATED_NEUTRAL.md) supplies the complete §504 text, damages findings and distinct fees remand. The [entering-law slice](../entering-law/OT_1997CHUNK6_A.md) supplies Markman, Gasperini and Hetzel at their precise current scope. The March 31 matters share a common predate substantive baseline. Almendarez-Torres supplies no constitutional majority to import; Woodard affects neither copyright allocation nor these remedies. The statutory ruling here stands on its own text and historical/functional inquiry.

## Stone's approved fixed core

The complete [Feltner supplement](../runtime/CHUNK6_SCOPED/feltner_v_columbia_pictures_television_inc_STONE.md) expressly adopts both the no-statutory-entitlement premise and the constitutional jury rule, including willfulness, amount, timely demand, retained legal/review functions and reserved equitable matters. He joins the complete lead and remedy, with no narrowing or fallback. His actual and approved reasons fit the reconciled seven-Associate constitutional path. No material premise has changed.

## Opinion form before assignment

One signed plenary merits opinion states the statutory premise and the resulting constitutional allocation, with a separate statutory-avoidance concurrence in the judgment. The two questions are actually necessary to that reasoning; no artificial partition or extra opinion is introduced for assignment. The nine-Justice reversing judgment has an eight-Justice rationale and Scalia's distinct statutory ground. No Marks construction is needed.

## Controlling law of the decision

### Section 504(c) supplies no independent statutory jury entitlement

**Holding and operative rule:** Section 504(c)'s authorization of statutory damages does not itself confer a right to a jury determination. That statutory conclusion does not settle the separate Seventh Amendment allocation.

**Authority:** Stone-Zsela's Opinion of the Court, joined by Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer: eight direct joins.

**Controlling explanation:** The provision supplies a damages election, ranges and specific conditions for adjustment. Its references to what the court considers just, the court's findings and its discretion contain no independent jury command. Reading those references in the context of the whole subsection yields no statutory entitlement to jury assessment. The contrary institutional reading of court cannot displace that conclusion merely to avoid the constitutional issue. The Court must therefore determine whether the Constitution preserves the jury's role despite the statute's allocation; statutory silence about a jury does not eliminate constitutional protection.

### The Seventh Amendment protects the initial determination of statutory-damages facts and amount

**Holding and operative rule:** On a timely jury demand in this private copyright statutory-damages action, the Seventh Amendment assigns disputed factual issues pertinent to the award, including willfulness and the amount within the lawful statutory range, to the jury. The court continues to interpret the statute, identify the lawful range, decide legal sufficiency and conduct constitutionally permissible review; the ruling does not assign injunctions, fees, costs, equitable accountings or historically judicial questions to juries.

**Authority:** The same eight Justices join the Court's constitutional holding and damages remand. Scalia supports the judgment on the separate statutory ground.

**Controlling explanation:** Copyright damages have a historical legal analogue, and the monetary remedy seeks compensation or punishment of the kind traditionally assessed by a jury. A range requiring judgment does not turn that task into equitable relief. Markman's historical and functional inquiry distinguishes a legal action's jury protection from the assignment of a particular legal-meaning function; its judicial patent-construction rule does not transfer disputed damages valuation to a judge.

Tull's allocation of the amount of a governmental civil penalty does not control this private copyright-damages function. Congress may identify the lawful range without removing the jury's task of deciding the pertinent facts and selecting the amount within it. Gasperini and Hetzel concern lawful review and the new-trial election after an award; they do not authorize initial judicial substitution for the demanded jury. Their applicable review limits remain intact.

Feltner demanded a jury, but the judge decided willfulness and the statutory amount. Those determinations cannot stand on that procedure. The remand changes the decisionmaker for the protected work, not the statute's ranges, burdens, per-work unit or exceptions. It does not resolve every challenge to the count of works, reopen unreviewed liability or guarantee any particular award.

**Operative statutory qualifications:** The owner may elect statutory damages before final judgment instead of actual damages and profits. The ordinary range is $500–$20,000 for all infringements of any one work for which one infringer is individually liable or two or more infringers are jointly and severally liable; all parts of a compilation or derivative work are one work. Owner-proved willfulness permits, but does not require, an increase to $100,000. Infringer-proved lack of awareness and of reason to believe the acts infringed permits, but does not require, reduction to no less than $200.

Mandatory remission is a separate rule. It requires belief, with reasonable grounds, that the use was fair use under §107, and either (1) reproduction in copies or phonorecords by an employee or agent of a nonprofit educational institution, library or archives acting within employment, or by that institution, library or archives itself; or (2) performance of a published nondramatic literary work, or reproduction of a transmission program embodying its performance, by a public broadcasting entity as defined in §118(g), or by a person as a regular part of that entity's nonprofit activities. Innocence or broadcaster status alone does not satisfy this rule. The Court finds no exception established here.

## Adaptive audit annex

### Frozen Associate commitments and historical comparison

## Feltner v. Columbia Pictures Television, Inc. — No. 96-1768 — March 31, 1998

**C — statutory premise and constitutional jury right:** Section 504(c)'s particular references to the court's findings, discretion and just award supply no statutory jury entitlement. The Seventh Amendment nevertheless protects jury determination, on demand, of the disputed statutory-damages issues and amount in this private legal damages action. Copyright damages have the relevant historical legal analogue; compensation, punishment and discretion within a range do not turn the remedy into equity. Tull's governmental civil-penalty allocation does not control this private damages valuation. Judicial legal interpretation and lawful review remain distinct from initial amount determination.

**T — statutory construction and avoidance:** Court can fairly mean the lawful tribunal, including its jury. Reading §504(c) to preserve jury determination of the damages facts and amount avoids an unnecessary constitutional ruling. This path does not adopt C's contrary statutory premise or decide the constitutional question.

| Justice | Final statutory/constitutional components and judgment | Individual reconciliation |
|---|---|---|
| Stevens | **C**; reverse denial of the demanded damages jury and remand. | His Tull separate join, Markman join and Gasperini position protect legal damages while allowing genuine legal correction. Historical C join matches; no need to adopt every Tull dictum or abandon his broader jury view. |
| O'Connor | **C**; same reversal/remand. | Her Tull majority join concerns government penalties; Markman, Gasperini and Hetzel distinguish other judicial functions. Historical C join confirms the material private-damages distinction. |
| Scalia | **T**; same judgment on statutory ground; constitutional question reserved. | His Tull writing and Gasperini dissent support the actual jury function. Historical concurrence, 355–359, uses the institutional reading of court, statutory history and avoidance; it expressly does not reach the constitutional issue. Preserve judgment-only agreement with C. |
| Kennedy | **C**; reverse and remand. | Markman, Gasperini and Hetzel joins preserve original factual valuation apart from construction/review. Historical C join remains compatible with that task-specific allocation. |
| Souter | **C**; reverse and remand. | His Markman and Gasperini opinions distinguish interpretation and review from protected factfinding. No changed premise displaces his historical C join. |
| Thomas | **C**; reverse and remand. | His Markman join and Gasperini dissent support historically distinct jury work. His historical statutory reading and constitutional allocation confirm C without importing authorship. |
| Ginsburg | **C**; reverse and remand. | Her Markman, Gasperini and Hetzel joins preserve the initial jury valuation. Her historical C join matches the frozen commitment with all §504(c)(2) qualifications retained. |
| Breyer | **C**; reverse and remand. | His Markman, Gasperini and Hetzel joins permit practical allocation inside the jury boundary. Historical C join supplies no basis for judicial original amount-setting here. |

**Coalitions and remedial limits:** Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer join C, including its statutory premise. Scalia joins T only; all eight support the reversing damages remedy. The historical Tull footnotes at 354–355 describe doubts and tension but do not overrule Tull; the operative distinction is sufficient. Historical Scalia's reference to the historical Almendarez-Torres dissent supplies no independent current-law authority; the avoidance principle is supported by pre-divergence authorities and his own position without importing that separate timeline's Court action.

The remedy does not reopen unreviewed infringement liability, decide the lawful work count, find willfulness or fix a sum. The 440 findings and $8.8 million award remain the lower-court account of the judgment being reversed in the reviewed respect. The separately vacated costs/fees award retains its remand. Section 504(c) retains the $500–$20,000 ordinary range per statutory work/liability unit and the compilation/derivative-work rule. Owner-proved willfulness permits, but does not require, an increase to $100,000; infringer-proved lack of awareness and reason to believe permits, but does not require, reduction to no less than $200. Mandatory remission separately requires belief, with reasonable grounds, that the use was fair use under ?107, and one of two qualifying circumstances: an employee or agent of a nonprofit educational institution, library or archives acting within the scope of employment, or the institution, library or archives itself, infringed by reproducing the work in copies or phonorecords; or a public broadcasting entity, or a person as a regular part of its nonprofit activities, infringed by performing a published nondramatic literary work or reproducing a transmission program embodying a performance of that work. Public broadcasting entity retains ?118(g)'s definition. Mere broadcaster status or innocent infringement does not satisfy that distinct rule. No exception is found established. No material historical departure remains.

### Final joins and assignment

Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer join every lead proposition with Stone. Scalia agrees only in the judgment and gives his frozen statutory explanation. No objection is treated as waived or answered by inventing a revised commitment. The statutory qualifications remain intact for all nine.

Chief Justice Stone-Zsela assigns from the unanimous disposition coalition. A fresh recount of actual opinion topologies, including Almendarez-Torres and Woodard, gives **Stone-Zsela 4; Stevens 5; O'Connor 7; Scalia 6; Kennedy 6; Souter 6; Thomas 5; Ginsburg 6; Breyer 6**; 51 counted leads. Last counted event: Ohio Adult Parole Authority v. Woodard, March 25, 1998, O'Connor. Eligible complete-lead authors: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. Scalia's judgment-only statutory route does not qualify. Minimum eligible count: 4; balance pool: Stone-Zsela (4), Stevens (5), Thomas (5).

Stone writes. His complete approved position precisely separates initial statutory-damages factfinding, willfulness and amount from statutory interpretation and lawful review. That separation supplies concrete fit for the opinion's actual task and its operative remand. Thomas is the strongest alternative because his Markman join and Gasperini dissent protect historical jury work; neither supplies a superior accommodation, since the eight share the complete formulation. Stone can achieve the common objective with the lower count and without changing any Associate's scope. Stevens's broader Tull concerns likewise require no accommodation in the adopted narrower private-damages holding. This is fit with no unresolved expansion problem, not a self-assignment based merely on subject interest. The lead adds one Stone count.

### Validation

Judgment 9–0; complete statutory and constitutional holdings eight direct joins; one separate judgment-only concurrence. Every exception's triggering conditions, permissive versus mandatory consequences, and relevant burdens are explicit. The rule does not convert the trial court's count or willfulness into Supreme Court findings. The controlling explanations are each below 350 words. No material departure from the historical Associate commitments or Court result remains, and no historical authorship is imported.

## Continuity and validation status

The Opinion Topology and Separate Writings below preserve every published material position for continuity at its stated scope; noncontrolling positions create no current law. The Procedure After Action block specifies the actual remaining stage. Final compatibility was tested against all eight frozen commitments and Stone’s complete approved supplement. assignment_statements.text:
**Case and dockets:** United States v. Scheffer, No. 96-1133.
**Event and date:** Merits decision, 1998-03-31; October Term 1997, chunk 6.
**Result:** Reversed and remanded, 8–1; categorical polygraph exclusion sustained against the presented constitutional challenge.
**Version / lineage:** Original decision; durable Record integrated into the current-term workspace. No repository commit is asserted.

## Event and law entering decision

Research cutoff: 1998-03-31. The authorized [neutral packet](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK6_A_VALIDATED_NEUTRAL.md) establishes review under §1259, the actual defense, government-administered examination, categorical exclusion and limited lower ruling. All nine Justices participate at both milestones; quorum and ordinary majority threshold are satisfied. The [entering-law slice](../entering-law/OT_1997CHUNK6_A.md) supplies the current Egelhoff protection/reservations and the actual Daubert/Joiner Rules holdings. Neither Almendarez-Torres nor Woodard changes this reliability inquiry. The March 31 cases share a predate substantive baseline; earlier same-date Record creation affects assignments only.

## Stone's approved core

The complete [Scheffer supplement](../runtime/CHUNK6_SCOPED/united_states_v_scheffer_STONE.md) sustains the categorical rule because serious reliability concerns remain, distinguishes excluding such evidence from impairing a meaningful defense, and directs reversal without inventing a trial result. Stone joins the entire common reliability lead and its bounded remedy. He joins neither additional-ground concurrence and is not attributed its grounds. No fallback or substantive extension of his approval occurs.

## Form-first determination

A single signed Court opinion states the common reliability ground. The three Associates who additionally support credibility-role and collateral-litigation justifications publish those grounds in a concurrence. Four Associates' distinct qualification is published because it defines their rejection of those additional grounds while preserving their full common-rule join. Stevens dissents. This arrangement reflects the governing and noncontrolling grounds actually supported before assignment; no proposition is added or divided to affect author eligibility. Every eight-Justice supporter can carry the complete common lead.

## Controlling law of the decision

### Supported reliability concerns justify this categorical polygraph rule against the presented constitutional challenge

**Holding and operative rule:** The constitutional right to present a defense permits evidentiary restrictions justified by legitimate trial interests and proportionate to their purposes. Serious, supported concerns about polygraph reliability justify Rule 707's categorical exclusion in this setting, where the accused can present his own factual account and underlying evidence; the Constitution does not require individualized admissibility proceedings for this credibility proffer.

**Authority:** Thomas's Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer: eight direct joins. The credibility-role and collateral-litigation rationales are separate, three-Justice grounds and do not become holdings.

**Controlling explanation:** Chambers and Rock protect a meaningful defense while allowing sufficiently justified evidentiary limits. Egelhoff applies that protection to rebuttal of the mental-state element actually retained by law and expressly preserves reliability restrictions. Here the rulemakers could respond to substantial disagreement about the reliability of polygraph conclusions with a uniform rule. An examiner's scientific certification that the accused is truthful differs from the accused's own account of the events. Scheffer testified to lack of knowing ingestion; Rule 707 did not remove that factual defense or deem the disputed element established.

The Government's administration of this examination and the importance of credibility do not establish that the Constitution requires an individualized foundation hearing. Daubert and Joiner govern the general Federal Rules' scientific-evidence inquiry; they do not constitutionalize that particular screening arrangement for every military evidence rule. The categorical form alone therefore does not make this restriction arbitrary or disproportionate.

The Court does not find that every polygraph is unreliable, determine an accuracy percentage, or resolve this test's truthfulness. Nor does permission to testify alone necessarily establish a complete defense in every case. The holding concerns this justified restriction and this proffer, leaving ordinary evidence rules and actual remaining claims intact. A separate Article 36(a) statutory-validity question is not decided.

**Rule's scope and exception:** Rule 707(a) excludes polygraph results, examiner opinions, and references to offering, failing to take or taking an examination. Rule 707(b) preserves statements made during an examination when they are otherwise admissible; it does not make every examination statement admissible.

## Adaptive audit annex

### Frozen commitments and historical reconciliation

## United States v. Scheffer — No. 96-1133 — March 31, 1998

### Reconciled components

**S — common constitutional ground:** The right to present a defense permits evidentiary restrictions justified by legitimate trial interests and proportionate to their purposes. The Constitution does not require individualized admissibility proceedings for this polygraph credibility proffer despite Rule 707's categorical form. The rulemakers' supported reliability concern, in the distinct setting of expert certification of truthfulness and with the accused's own factual account available, supplies sufficient justification. Daubert and Joiner interpret the general Rules; they do not constitutionally mandate that regime for every military rule. Rule 707(b) continues to preserve otherwise admissible statements made during an examination. Reverse the CAAF's constitutional judgment and return for consistent proceedings.

**B and C — additional category-specific justifications:** In this polygraph setting, preserving court members' responsibility to judge credibility against a scientifically presented certification of the accused's truthfulness is an additional adequate justification for a categorical rule; so is avoiding the recurring collateral litigation over examiner qualifications, question design, countermeasures and interpretation. These positions permit this rule, not all exclusion of expert evidence bearing on credibility or any defense evidence that consumes time. They are separately joined only as identified below.

**F — opposing constitutional ground:** A total prohibition prevents a showing that a significant defense proffer is sufficiently reliable. Government administration of this examination and the proffer's relation to knowing ingestion make the opportunity consequential. The meaningful-defense protection in Egelhoff and Rock requires lawful foundation review here, without compelling ultimate admission, acquittal or a new trial before that inquiry. Affirm the constitutional rejection of the per se obstacle and preserve lawful further proceedings.

| Justice | Final reach, judgment and exact grounds joined | Historical reconciliation and prior individual anchor |
|---|---|---|
| Stevens | Reach constitutional question; **F**; affirm removal of categorical obstacle. No independent Article 36(a) disposition. | His Egelhoff join, Breyer concurrence join and Joiner separate writing support assessing the actual defense and proffer. Historical dissent, 320–339, independently agrees with constitutional invalidity and discusses Article 36(a), but at 325 expressly does not rest on the unbriefed statutory ground. Preserve that concern as a reservation, not an alternative holding or a command to admit this test. |
| O'Connor | Reach; reverse and return on **S**; decline B and C as independent grounds. | Her Rock dissent join permits justified categorical scientific-evidence rules; Egelhoff preserves real reliability limits. Historical join of Parts I, II-A and II-D and of the qualification at 318–320 confirms the common ground and refusal of the additional grounds. |
| Scalia | Reach; reverse and return; join **S, B and C**. | His Rock dissent and Egelhoff dissent support this rulemaking latitude, while Daubert/Joiner do not constitutionalize their design. Historical complete join confirms all three justifications at the stated category-specific level. |
| Kennedy | Reach; reverse and return on **S**; decline B and C as independent grounds. | His Egelhoff dissent and Joiner opinion preserve justified evidentiary regulation. Historical qualification, 318–320, rejects the purported need to shield the jury from ultimate-issue assistance and relies on reasonable reliability disagreement. This matches the provisional limitation. |
| Souter | Reach; reverse and return; join **S, B and C**. **Corrected from provisional contextual-only treatment of B/C.** | His Egelhoff concurrence expressly reserved convincing evidentiary justification; Daubert/Joiner were general-Rules holdings. Historically he joined II-B and II-C as well as the common portions. The current Egelhoff rule does not erase credibility-role or collateral-litigation justifications for this special proffer. No source establishes that he now rejects those grounds, and neither changing the Chief nor a generic citation to Egelhoff suffices. His exact historical join is therefore the stronger supported commitment. |
| Thomas | Reach; reverse and return; join **S, B and C**. | His Egelhoff dissent and Daubert/Joiner joins permit justified regulation without turning screening rules into constitutional requirements. The historical complete rationale agrees with the frozen category-specific commitment. |
| Ginsburg | Reach; reverse and return on **S**; decline B and C as independent grounds. | Her Egelhoff position concerns genuine culpability definition rather than arbitrary exclusion of retained-element rebuttal; reliability here is a different sufficient justification. Her historical partial join and qualification at 318–320 support preserving the refusal of a jury-monopoly rationale. |
| Breyer | Reach; reverse and return on **S**; decline B and C as independent grounds. | His Egelhoff concurrence protects actual mental-state testing and Joiner concurrence favors practical assessment, without mandatory hearing architecture. His historical partial join accepts constitutional permission despite policy doubts and supports the same limited position. |

**Proposition coalitions:** O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer join S. Scalia, Souter and Thomas additionally join B and C. Stevens alone supports F among Associates. O'Connor, Kennedy, Ginsburg and Breyer may publish a shared partial-join qualification if B/C are published: policy doubts about per se exclusion, the possibility of a stronger future proffer, and the difference between constitutional permission and evidentiary wisdom do not change their present judgment. If only S is published, their disagreement must not be converted into unstated B/C joins. Authorship remains unassigned.

**Reason for reconciliation change:** Souter's original narrower position was legally possible, but no concrete changed factual, remedial, statutory or personal public-position premise supports departure from his actual historical B/C joins. Egelhoff expressly preserved sufficiently justified evidence limits, and his own concurrence did so too. The correction follows full review of the historical partial-join structure and current-law reservations, rather than treating unanimity on a general right to defend as a mechanical vote rule. It changes no judgment and creates no new source fact.

**Footnotes, scientific limits and remedy:** The historical majority's scientific surveys and Stevens's competing accuracy figures are opposing evidentiary characterizations, not newly adopted neutral scientific findings. The current decision need not decide any percentage or the accuracy of Scheffer's test. Historical note 11 confirms that the CAAF removed the per se obstacle; it did not itself guarantee admissibility. Note 13 marks the dispute between a credibility opinion and factual evidence; F disputes that characterization's constitutional significance, and S does not assert that every testimony-permitted trial necessarily affords a complete defense. Stevens's Article 36(a) discussion remains provisional because its practicability and consistency conditions and unbriefed scope prevent an independent disposition. Historical Kennedy's discussion of Rule 704 identifies the objection to B, not a holding invalidating Rule 707. Neither path invents the CAAF mandate, reinstates all counts and sentence automatically, commands a new trial, or resolves unpresented statutory validity. No final material historical departure remains.

### Final compatibility and balanced assignment

All seven reversing Associates join the full reliability ground with Stone. Souter's reconciled additional B/C joins are preserved in Scalia's concurrence with Thomas; they are not lost by moving those noncontrolling grounds out of the lead. O'Connor, Kennedy, Ginsburg and Breyer retain the opposite qualification, and Stevens retains F. No Associate commitment changes at assembly, no new scientific finding appears, and no invented circulation history supplies a join.

Chief Justice Stone-Zsela assigns. Fresh recount from actual copied and newly written opinion topologies gives **Stone-Zsela 5; Stevens 5; O'Connor 7; Scalia 6; Kennedy 6; Souter 6; Thomas 5; Ginsburg 6; Breyer 6**; total 52. Last counted event: Feltner, March 31, 1998, Stone-Zsela. Texas is a signed threshold disposition and adds no count. Eligible authors for the complete common lead: Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. Minimum: 5. Pool: Stone-Zsela (5), Scalia (6), Kennedy (6), Souter (6), Thomas (5), Ginsburg (6), Breyer (6). O'Connor (7) is eligible but outside the pool.

Thomas writes for fit. His actual Daubert/Joiner joins and Egelhoff position distinguish the authority to regulate evidence from a compulsory constitutional screening design, the central legal work here. He can state the common reliability ground while preserving his additional category-specific grounds through a separate join. Stone is the strongest equal-count alternative: his approved position states the same distinction precisely. Thomas's supported treatment of rulemaking latitude and the statutory/constitutional boundary offers a concrete advantage in explaining why the general Rules do not displace the military rule, without requiring Stone to adopt additional justifications. No necessary join depends on a new accommodation, so this is fit rather than expansion. Scalia's own Rock/Egelhoff positions fit the additional-ground concurrence; Kennedy's frozen qualification fits the four-Justice concurrence. Only Thomas's lead counts.

### Validation

Eight judgment supporters, eight complete lead joins, three additional-ground concurrence joins, four qualifying concurrence joins and one dissent reconcile without double-counting. Souter's two reconciled additional joins remain explicit. No statutory disposition under Article 36(a) or individualized reliability finding is supplied. The ordinary explanation is below 350 words. assignment_statements.text:
**Case and dockets:** United States v. United States Shoe Corp., No. 97-372.
**Event and date:** Merits decision, 1998-03-31; October Term 1997, chunk 6.
**Result:** Affirmed, 9–0; CIT residual jurisdiction and export-refund judgment sustained.
**Version / lineage:** Original decision; durable Record integrated into the current-term workspace. No repository commit is asserted.

## Event, sources and entering law

Research cutoff: 1998-03-31. Certiorari review under §1254(1), all nine participants at argument and decision, quorum present and five votes required. The [validated neutral packet](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK6_A_VALIDATED_NEUTRAL.md) supplies the record and limits; the separate [jurisdiction supplement](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK6_SHOE_JURISDICTION_VALIDATED.md) supplies the complete relevant statutory language and verified date-eligible text. The later publication used to copy unchanged §1581 provisions is not a later substantive amendment or in-world event. Actual present law is the IBM and Northwest Airlines material in [the entering-law slice](../entering-law/OT_1997CHUNK6_A.md), with Steel Co.'s threshold discipline. The predate substantive baseline is shared with other March 31 events. Almendarez-Torres and Woodard alter no pertinent premise; same-day author counting imports no substantive dependency.

## Stone's fixed core and final joins

The complete [Shoe supplement](../runtime/CHUNK6_SCOPED/united_states_v_united_states_shoe_corp_STONE.md) expressly adopts residual CIT jurisdiction before the merits, identifies no applicable more-specific subsection, applies IBM and Pace to the value-based export levy, and affirms the bounded refund. Its nonexport and genuine-service reservations remain explicit. Stone joins the complete lead without fallback or substantive alteration. The statutory jurisdiction direction and constitutional classification remain distinct, as his approved sequence requires.

## Form-first determination

A single signed plenary merits opinion resolves the necessary statutory jurisdiction and the export-tax question, with one unanimous affirmance and no separate writing. Both legal steps are independently necessary to this disposition; the parts reflect those steps rather than an assignment adjustment. Every Justice joins every governing proposition.

## Controlling law of the decision

### I. The Court of International Trade has exclusive residual jurisdiction over this levy challenge

**Holding and operative rule:** Section 1581(i)(4), read with §1581(i)(1) and 26 U.S.C. §4462(f)(2), gives the Court of International Trade exclusive jurisdiction over this challenge to administration and enforcement of the Harbor Maintenance Tax. The challenge attacks the legislatively fixed exaction rather than a protestable Customs decision under §1514, so §1581(a)'s protest-denial channel is not the necessary route.

**Authority:** Ginsburg's Opinion of the Court, joined by all eight other Justices: nine direct joins.

**Controlling explanation:** Congress directs that the levy be treated as a customs duty for jurisdictional purposes. The statute provides revenue from imports as well as imposing other applications of the same levy; §1581(i)(4) covers its administration and enforcement. That direction supplies the appropriate exclusive forum before the constitutional question is reached.

Section 1581(a) concerns denial of a protest against a Customs decision of the kind governed by §1514. Here Customs passively collected a charge fixed by Congress; its form response did not supply a discretionary valuation, classification or other decision that determines this constitutional challenge. A document called a protest does not change the action's nature. Residual jurisdiction therefore does not excuse a missed protest deadline or circumvent an otherwise governing specific channel.

Section 1581(i)'s exclusion for specified antidumping or countervailing determinations reviewable by the Court of International Trade or the designated binational panels, and §1581(j)'s exclusion of actions under Tariff Act §305, do not encompass this levy claim. Section 4462(f)(1)'s regulation-qualified application of customs administration and its penalty rule, and (f)(3)'s exclusion of internal-revenue administration, remain distinct from (f)(2)'s jurisdictional direction. Calling the levy a customs duty for jurisdiction does not decide its constitutional character.

### II. The value-based charge on export loading is an export tax, not a compensatory service fee

**Holding and operative rule:** The Export Clause prohibits this Harbor Maintenance Tax as applied to exports because its ad valorem assessment does not fairly measure services or facilities used by the exporter. A genuine compensatory charge may use reasonable administrative approximations, but dedicated revenue and a general connection to useful harbor work do not convert a cargo-value export tax into a permissible fee.

**Authority:** The same nine Justices join the Court's merits holding and affirmance of the export-refund judgment.

**Controlling explanation:** IBM establishes that nondiscrimination cannot save a federal tax on exports. The Government accordingly defends this levy as a user fee. Pace permits compensation for actual governmental services and safeguards, allowing workable approximation rather than exact individualized billing. The distinction turns on the charge's relationship to the service, not its name.

The levy imposes 0.125 percent of cargo value at export loading. Its receipts enter a dedicated harbor-maintenance fund, but cargo value does not fairly measure the exporter's use of the relevant facilities or services. The fund's useful purpose supplies no missing relationship between the tax base and that use. The Court need not invent a benefit ratio or find each particular payment excessive to identify this structural defect.

Northwest Airlines concerns a different statutory airport-fee regime and does not replace the Export Clause with a general reasonableness or nondiscrimination test. IBM's service reservations likewise do not exempt every charge related to shipping. This decision concerns the uncontested goods in export transit and the export payments claimed. It reaches neither import or domestic applications, nor a differently measured service fee, nor general taxes on legally independent events. Reasonable inspection, storage, wharfage and facility-use charges are not prohibited by this holding.

## Adaptive audit annex

### Frozen Associate commitments and reconciliation

## United States v. United States Shoe Corp. — No. 97-372 — March 31, 1998

**J — jurisdiction:** Section 1581(i)(4), read with (i)(1) and §4462(f)(2), gives the CIT exclusive jurisdiction over this administration/enforcement challenge to the HMT exaction. Congress directs customs-duty treatment for jurisdiction; the law also provides revenue from imports. The constitutional challenge attacks the legislatively fixed exaction, not a discretionary Customs valuation or classification decision. Passive collection and a form response do not make it a §1514 protestable decision merely because the company filed a document called a protest. Section 1581(a) therefore is not the necessary channel here. No untimely-protest cure or new deadline exception is adopted.

**M — export-tax merits:** IBM excludes nondiscrimination as a defense to a real federal tax upon exports. Pace preserves genuine compensation for government services, with workable approximation, but a charge must fairly correspond to the exporter's use of the services and facilities rather than tax protected cargo under a service label. This 0.125-percent value-only levy attaches to export loading; earmarking its receipts for useful harbor work does not supply the missing service-related measure. It is an export tax as applied here. Affirm the existing export-refund judgment.

| Justice | Final jurisdiction, merits and remedy | Individual historical reconciliation |
|---|---|---|
| Stevens | **J and M**; affirm. | His Northwest Airlines join permits genuine facility charges, while Pace supplies the applicable export distinction. He did not participate in IBM, but its law governs; no prior view is invented. His historical unanimous join matches these components. |
| O'Connor | **J and M**; affirm. | Her IBM and Northwest Airlines joins distinguish an actual export tax from a service charge; Steel Co. supports establishing J first. The historical join has no displaced premise. |
| Scalia | **J and M**; affirm. | His IBM and Northwest Airlines joins reject a mere nondiscrimination answer while allowing properly justified fees; Steel Co. supports the channel inquiry. Historical agreement remains supported. |
