**Case and dockets:** Breard v. Greene, application A-732, associated petition No. 97-8214.
**Event and date:** Court order on referred stay application, 1998-04-14; October Term 1997, chunk 6.
**Result:** A-732 denied, 6–3; no accompanying petition or companion action.
**Version / lineage:** Original decision of the previously open A-732 application. User-supplied lineage: c964d3b2 (open matter), 3d3224a4 (approved operative Stone supplement); no Git verification is claimed. The separate completed A-738/A-767/A-771 Record is not replaced or amended.

## Event, route and participation

The March 30 application requests a stay of the execution scheduled for 9 p.m. April 14 pending certiorari in No. 97-8214, seeking review of the first federal habeas judgment. The application reports a March 23 request below and March 27 denial. It identifies the treaty/default and separate proportionality-method due-process claims. No final petition poll, petition disposition or execution fact is inferred. The standing practice and Fourth Circuit allotment send A-732 to Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and through his referral to the Court. All nine Justices participate at referral and decision, no absence or recusal being established; quorum six and majority five govern the application, independently of certiorari's four-vote rule.

Rules 22 and 23 are read in their complete 1995 form in the authorized source-text sections of [the validated neutral treaty packet](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK6_BREARD_VALIDATED_NEUTRAL.md). Rule 23's ordinary request-below requirement and most-extraordinary-circumstances exception remain distinct. Missing reproduced exhibits are a source limitation, not proof that the application lacked required papers or service. No temporary action or new substitute Justice is invented. Section 10's signed statements, Circuit Justice explanation and Chief certification are supplied by this Record; the administrative certification adds no reason or vote.

## Current law and source cutoff

The [final neutral packet](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK6_RESUMED_NEUTRAL.md), §4, supplies the supported facts, claims, C/E terms, party disputes and limits. The complete Article 36 text in the authorized prior neutral source establishes separate advice, request-based notification, communication and access rights, the expressly-opposed-action limit, and both clauses of paragraph (2). The [entering-law slice](../entering-law/OT_1997CHUNK6_RESUMED.md) supplies Coleman's May 20, 1992 interim test, the surviving 1991 default law, and the exact modules “Interim protection necessary for required habeas process” and “No delay-based substitute for statutory habeas dismissal” (Lonchar, April 1, 1996). No independent unfinished legal duty is established here.

The first federal petition was filed in August 1996 after AEDPA. The exact “State-court merits decisions and factual development under amended §2254” and “Exhaustion and merits denial under amended §2254” modules have April 24, 1996 operative statutory authority; Lindh's June 23, 1997 pending-noncapital holding does not exempt this filing. Section 2254(d) requires a state merits adjudication of this claim. Section 2254(e)(1) supplies the actual state-fact presumption and clear-and-convincing rebuttal; §2254(e)(2) has its distinct failure-to-develop trigger, alternative previously unavailable retroactive constitutional rule or undiscoverable-with-due-diligence factual predicate, and cumulative clear-and-convincing guilt condition. Chapter 154 qualification is not established. These are preserved legal limits, not invented final grounds for rejecting the application.

“Sequencing nonretroactivity and procedural default on habeas review” (Lambrix, May 12, 1997) and “Late assertion of Teague nonretroactivity” (Schiro, January 19, 1994, with Caspari's distinct preserved-defense comparison February 23) preserve actual presentation and finality inquiries. Both contemporary exceptions remain: substantive limits on the State's punishment power and watershed procedures essential to fundamental accuracy and fairness. O'Dell's June 19, 1997 exception is confined to its future-dangerousness, actual legal parole-ineligibility and denied-effective-correction conjunction. No later rule or new Woodard holding is treated as law at Breard's finality. Woodard's March 25 actual decision informs the current adjudication/mercy distinction without establishing a retrospective database rule.

Dorsainvil's threshold dismissal supplies no new barrier to this first-habeas review application; Bird's component-specific liveness rule does not change the imminent relief requested here. Neither same-day companion adjudication supplies antecedent A-732 law. Research cutoff: April 14, 1998, before this action. The completed companion Record remains byte-identical; this order imposes no change in its protection, disposition or next stage.

## Material record and unresolved predicates

The stipulated failure to advise is distinct from cause, enforceability, prejudice and remedy. The plea advice/refusal/testimony account is supported but the effect of consular assistance remains contested. The Fourth Circuit rejected cause and expressly did not reach prejudice. District Claim IV, 949 F. Supp. 1255, 1266–67, quotes the preserved federal method argument and rejects Slayton default; its substantive, §2254(d) and Teague grounds are lower reasons, not imported Supreme Court holdings. The parties dispute the Fourth Circuit's treatment. The separate substantive disproportionate-sentence claims cannot supply Claim IV's default.

Section C requires arbitrary-influence and similar-crime/defendant proportionality determinations. Section E permits time-bounded accumulation, commands use of available records as a guide, and commands availability of accumulated records to circuit courts. The state court's reported comparison of reviewed capital cases including life sentences is its method and conclusion, not a statutory command or proof of a complete universe. The 33/19/14/two figures, varying date range and newspaper-derived descriptions are filing allegations with untested comparability. No statistical constitutional entitlement is inferred. Supported published recitations and authenticated judicial quotations are used at their stated scope under Engine §14; original unsupplied exhibits and whole-code amendment history are not claimed as read. No gap is litigant misconduct.

## Form, authorship and final signed joins

One reasoned referred-application order addresses the two actual grounds, with the Circuit Justice's signed explanation divided into the common stay standard, treaty assessment and separate process assessment. The genuine scope differences require Souter's concurrence and Stevens's dissent with an additional process part. This form follows the interim legal work before counts or author consideration. Stone's authorship of his own explanation is imposed by the Fourth Circuit allotment under Engine §10, not assigned under §8. Its adopted Parts I/II/III are respectively 9/5/8-Justice Court portions; no other lead explanation requires assignment. Application explanations and all separate writings add no balanced-assignment count.

O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas adopt the complete explanation at the precise T1/P1 scope in their frozen rows. Souter joins Parts I and III only, preserving his reconciled independent treaty-causation ground. Ginsburg and Breyer join Parts I and III and Stevens's treaty dissent, but not his process-sufficiency part. Stevens joins the common standard and supplies both his dissent grounds. Every adopted paragraph is compatible with each Justice's recorded position; no stronger default, prejudice, statutory-method, AEDPA or Teague holding is introduced to create a join. The common process insufficiency does not become support by Ginsburg or Breyer for the final denial. No material Associate commitment changes in assembly, so no post-circulation historical-departure audit is triggered.

## Stone fixed-core and scope check

The approved core denies interim relief under Coleman on the treaty/default showing while preserving possible enforceability and ultimate prejudice. Its distinct process reason applies Pulley/Lewis and Hicks without defaulting Claim IV or deciding state law. Those supplied grounds support his entire explanation at this limited interim scope. Stone adopts no categorical treaty bar, presumed habeas-hearing failure, final new-rule determination or accompanying petition result. No fallback is used; the separate explanation duty is met by approved reasons for both actual claims. His certification uses the prescribed administrative form and creates no substantive choice.

## Public action, law and continuity

Application A-732 is denied, 6–3. Supporting denial: Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter and Thomas. Opposing denial: Stevens, Ginsburg and Breyer.

The denial issues no stay under A-732. It does not dissolve an unidentified order, independently authorize an execution, grant or deny petition No. 97-8214, or act on any companion proceeding. The separate process claim is insufficient for a stay by eight stated positions, including Ginsburg and Breyer, who nevertheless support protection on the treaty ground. The five joins in the Court's treaty analysis remain distinct from Souter's independent ground.

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Scope and relationship |
|---|---|---|---|
| Circuit Justice's signed explanation; opinion of the Court, Part I | Stone-Zsela | Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | Governing stay standard; no final petition vote |
| Same explanation; opinion of the Court, Part II | Stone-Zsela | O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas | Treaty/default interim insufficiency; supports denial |
| Same explanation; opinion of the Court, Part III | Stone-Zsela | O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | Separate process-claim interim insufficiency; Ginsburg and Breyer favor the stay on another ground |
| Concurrence in denial | Souter | No other Justice | Independent treaty causal/remedial obstacle; joins Court Parts I and III, not II |
| Dissent, Part I | Stevens | Ginsburg, Breyer | Would grant the defined stay on treaty review/reversal prospects |
| Dissent, Part II | Stevens | No other Justice | Independent process-claim basis for the same stay |

Each participating Justice's signed adoption or separate statement is specified below. The Chief Justice's explanation arises from the Fourth Circuit allotment; its majority-joined portions are the Court's opinion, not a separate concurrence.

#### I. The stay requires both meaningful review prospects and irreparable harm

**Holding and operative rule.** A stay of execution pending certiorari requires a reasonable probability that four Justices would accept review, a significant possibility of reversal and likely irreparable harm without protection. Execution's irreversibility supplies the last requirement, but does not dispense with the two review requirements or independently overcome an applicable barrier to relief.

**Authority.** Chief Justice Stone-Zsela's signed Circuit Justice explanation, Part I, joined by all eight Associates, states the Court's governing interim standard. These joins reveal no final vote on the pending petition.

**Controlling explanation.** The Court applies Coleman v. Thompson, decided May 20, 1992, which uses Barefoot's distinct requirements for protection pending review. The issue is whether the actual claims and legally available remedies justify a stay, not whether execution is serious or the asserted violation deserves attention. Each claim requires its own assessment, including any independent obstacle to a legally consequential reversal. The Court's decision on this application does not decide the petition or finally adjudicate the claims. Lonchar protects process actually required by law when lawful expedition cannot complete it before execution; first-petition status and difficulty alone establish no unfinished legal duty or automatic pause.

#### II. The present treaty/default showing does not justify a stay

**Holding and operative rule.** On this submission, the asserted Vienna Convention notification violation does not establish a sufficient prospect of obtaining relief through the surviving default and remedial barriers to justify a stay. The treaty source and asserted novelty of a claim do not alone establish cause, prejudice or an applicable exception; this interim conclusion neither makes every consular claim unenforceable nor decides ultimate prejudice.

**Authority.** Chief Justice Stone-Zsela's Part II, joined by O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas, supplies five direct joins to this sufficient treaty-ground assessment. Souter supports denial on the distinct causal/remedial assessment in his concurrence and does not join Part II.

**Controlling explanation.** Article 36 requires advice without delay of the detained person's consular rights, notification to the consulate on request, and forwarding of communications without delay. Consular assistance rights coexist with the duty to refrain if the national expressly opposes action. Paragraph (2) permits receiving-State procedures subject to their enabling full effect to the rights' purposes. The Court gives that proviso weight: failure to give notice can bear on timely exercise of the right. But the proviso does not itself establish that this applicant could not have presented the available claim with reasonable diligence, that novelty supplies external cause, or that correction of the alleged violation permits the requested domestic remedy. Coleman (1991), Carrier and Reed require those distinct inquiries; treaty supremacy does not collapse them. The stipulated notice failure does not concede prejudice. Counsel's advice to accept a noncapital offer, Breard's refusal and his choice to testify leave the asserted different effect of consular advice disputed. The Fourth Circuit rejected cause without deciding prejudice. The Court makes no final contrary factual finding and does not say consular advice could never change a defense. The present submission does not show the required prospect of legally consequential relief past those obstacles. A notification allegation alone also supplies no reliable new innocence evidence satisfying Schlup.

#### III. The separate challenge to Virginia's proportionality-review method does not independently justify a stay

**Holding and operative rule.** The present claim that Virginia administered its statutory proportionality review through an inadequate comparison pool does not show sufficient reversal prospects to support a stay. State-law error alone is not a federal habeas ground; a genuine arbitrary deprivation of a state-created sentencing entitlement remains a distinct federal question, but this submission does not adequately demonstrate such a deprivation.

**Authority.** Chief Justice Stone-Zsela's Part III, joined by O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer, supplies eight direct joins. Ginsburg and Breyer nevertheless support a stay on the treaty ground. Stevens alone regards the process claim as independently sufficient for protection.

**Controlling explanation.** Pulley rejects a universal federal requirement of comparative proportionality review, and Lewis v. Jeffers does not authorize federal correction of state-law error alone. Hicks preserves protection against arbitrary deprivation of an existing sentencing entitlement. This claim therefore cannot be dismissed merely by confusing it with a different claim that the sentence itself was disproportionate. The district court recognized the federal method claim and expressly rejected default before denying relief; the parties dispute how the Fourth Circuit treated it. Virginia's §17-110.1(C) requires determinations concerning arbitrary influence and excessiveness or disproportionality compared with similar crimes and defendants. Subsection (E) permits collection within a period the court chooses, requires consideration of available records as a guide, and requires accumulated records to be available to circuit courts. Permission to accumulate records is not a command to collect every prosecution. The state court reported examining capital cases it reviewed, including life sentences. That account is not proof of an exhaustive comparison, but the offered aggregate sentencing figures likewise do not establish which crimes and defendants are legally similar or that the required determination was rendered arbitrary. The objection thus disputes how review was performed without adequately showing deprivation of the review or substantive protection the statute supplies. The Court decides no state-law construction or final due-process merits question. The possible appellate claim-treatment error does not by itself establish sufficient prospects of relief despite the independent weaknesses of the asserted federal deprivation.

#### Limits of the interim decision

The Court decides neither categorical individual treaty enforceability, ultimate cause or prejudice, a final default exception, nor the merits of the separate proportionality-method claim. It does not attribute the substantive sentence claim's default to District Claim IV. No blanket AEDPA hearing bar, hearing entitlement, chapter 154 qualification, final §2254(d) determination or Teague disposition is adopted. Section 2254(d) requires an actual state merits adjudication of the relevant claim; a federal district court's merits discussion alone does not supply one. If the applicant failed to develop the claim's factual basis in state proceedings, §2254(e)(2) bars a federal evidentiary hearing unless the claim relies on either a previously unavailable new constitutional rule made retroactive on collateral review by this Court or a factual predicate not previously discoverable through due diligence, and the underlying facts would establish clearly and convincingly that, but for constitutional error, no reasonable factfinder would have found the applicant guilty of the underlying offense. No finding of that failure or satisfaction of those exceptions is made here. Teague's actual presentation and finality inquiries, its exception for substantive limits on the State's power to punish conduct or classes of persons, and its exception for watershed procedures essential to fundamental accuracy and fairness retain their separate predicates. Nothing in this order resolves the accompanying certiorari petition, original habeas proceeding, original-action motion or other emergency applications.

- Coleman v. Thompson, 504 U.S. 188 (1992), and Barefoot v. Estelle, 463 U.S. 880 (1983), are applied to the separate review-prospect and irreparable-harm requirements, without creating an automatic capital stay.
- Coleman v. Thompson, 501 U.S. 722 (1991), Murray v. Carrier, 477 U.S. 478 (1986), and Reed v. Ross, 468 U.S. 1 (1984), supply default, external-cause and legal-novelty principles for the limited treaty assessment. No categorical treaty exception or prohibition is announced.
- Pulley v. Harris, 465 U.S. 37 (1984), rejects a universal comparative-review requirement; Lewis v. Jeffers, 497 U.S. 764 (1990), limits federal relief for state-law error alone; Hicks v. Oklahoma, 447 U.S. 343 (1980), preserves the distinct arbitrary-deprivation question. Their separate functions are retained.
- Lonchar v. Thomas, 517 U.S. 314 (1996), remains protection for identified, legally required habeas process that cannot be completed by lawful expedition, not an automatic stay of every first petition. Schlup v. Delo, decided January 23, 1995, retains its reliable-new-evidence probability gateway; an asserted lost opportunity for consular assistance does not itself satisfy it.
- Trest v. Cain, decided December 9, 1997, creates no duty to invent an omitted default defense and does not remove the treaty default actually asserted here. Ohio Adult Parole Authority v. Woodard, decided March 25, 1998, and Doe v. District of Columbia, decided June 2, 1997, establish neither a universal comparison database nor the absence of every independent judicial-process claim.
- Lambrix v. Singletary, decided May 12, 1997, and O'Dell v. Netherland, decided June 19, 1997, preserve claim-specific nonretroactivity analysis. O'Dell's confined future-dangerousness, legal-parole-ineligibility and denied-corrective-opportunity holding is not a general capital-procedure exception. No final nonretroactivity determination is made here.

The action applies current interim law without a final new treaty/default, proportionality-method, AEDPA or retroactivity merits rule. Direct 9/5/8 support establishes the exact interim propositions; no Marks synthesis combines Souter's distinct treaty rationale with Part II. The signed positions and their noncontrolling grounds are preserved in the Public Projection. A-732 is resolved; petition No. 97-8214 remains unadjudicated by this event. No new protection, expiration or removal of another order is supplied, and no completed execution is imported. The narrow interim decision changes no gateway, disclosure or acquisition premise in Carriger; the later packet requires no clean refresh from this action alone. Parent term-wide dependency review remains separate.

## Adaptive audit annex

The following final individual components and reconciliation are script-copied from the immutable [reconciled handoff](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK6_RESUMED_RECONCILED.md); the [fresh commitments](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK6_RESUMED_COMMITMENTS.md) preserve the underlying alternative comparisons. Souter's final reconciled position, not his superseded provisional position, controls assembly.

## 4. Breard v. Greene, A-732 — April 14, 1998

### Shared legal and source boundaries

A-732 seeks a stay pending petition No. 97-8214, not a writ or final petition action. Coleman (May 20, 1992), applying Barefoot, requires a reasonable probability that four Members would accept review, a significant possibility of reversal and likely irreparable harm. Execution is irreversible but does not alone satisfy the first two requirements. A review-prospect assessment is not a final certiorari vote; a Court stay requires the participating majority. Lonchar supplies no automatic first-petition stay or process to complete merely because the case is difficult.

Article 36(1)(b)'s advice-without-delay duty is distinct from consular notification on request and forwarding communications; paragraph (1)(c)'s assistance rights preserve abstention if expressly opposed. Article 36(2) permits receiving-State procedure subject to enabling full effect to the rights' purposes. The notice failure is stipulated; individual enforceability, default, cause, prejudice and remedy remain separate. Counsel's advice to accept a noncapital offer and Breard's contrary choices make the alleged effect of consular advice disputed, not disproved as a historical fact. The Fourth Circuit rejected cause without reaching prejudice. Neither treaty supremacy alone nor unfamiliarity with available law establishes a default exception.

District Claim IV expressly recognizes the distinct federal proportionality-method theory and rejects Slayton default before denying relief. Claim III C's treatment cannot be copied onto it. The parties dispute whether the Fourth Circuit addressed Claim IV; petitioner’s allegation of omission is not an undisputed appellate finding. The relevant text separately requires C's determinations concerning arbitrary influence and excessiveness/disproportionality against similar crimes and defendants; E permits accumulation within a chosen period, requires consideration of available records as a guide, and requires accumulated records to be available to circuit courts. It commands no universal collection. The state court's account of reviewing appealed capital cases, including life sentences, is its method and conclusion, not proof of a complete universe. The 33/19/14/two figures and newspaper-derived descriptions remain filing allegations, not verified comparability or a constitutional sentencing rate.

Hicks/Evitts's substantive/adjudicatory protection argument and Pulley's rejection of universal comparative review remain distinct. Doe and Woodard prevent mandatory procedure alone from creating a substantive entitlement; Woodard also preserves a retained-life minimum and the distinction between executive mercy and adjudication. Neither creates an exhaustive-database rule or supplies law at an earlier finality date. The state-law construction does not itself extinguish a genuinely independent federal claim.

Amended §2254(d) requires a relevant state merits adjudication; a federal district merits discussion supplies none. Section 2254(e)(2) has its own failure-to-develop trigger, alternative new-rule or due-diligence factual predicate, and cumulative clear-and-convincing guilt condition. No categorical hearing bar or hearing entitlement is adopted. Chapter 154 qualification is unestablished. Teague's actual presentation, finality inquiry and both contemporary exceptions retain their independent terms. Lambrix/O'Dell reject blanket treatment but establish no comparison-universe entitlement; O'Dell's watershed holding remains confined to future dangerousness, actual legal parole ineligibility and denied effective correction of a misleading release premise. No Justice here decides the unresolved predicates needed for final habeas relief.

### Final individual commitments

| Associate | Treaty/default component | Separate proportionality-method component | Final relief position and reconciliation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stevens | Retain T2: the actual relationship between notice, full effect and default supplies sufficient review/reversal prospects for interim protection. Novelty alone, enforceability, causal prejudice and ultimate remedy are not decided. | Retain P2 as an independently sufficient stay ground: the preserved adjudicatory theory and possible failure to address it warrant review without requiring every capital record or finding arbitrary review proved. | Grant a stay tied to petition disposition. His authored Lonchar, Woodard dissent seeking a bounded process inquiry even in clemency, and Lambrix/O'Dell joins support these limited grounds. Historical stay support confirms the relief direction; the historical writing's ordinary-deliberation concern is not converted into an automatic timing entitlement or represented as a published Claim IV rationale. |
| O'Connor | Retain T1: ordinary diligence/default and independent remedy obstacles leave insufficient significant possibility of reversal on this submission; the full-effect proviso must still be considered. | Retain P1: actual comparative review and the limited, untested pool showing do not establish sufficient prospects of arbitrary deprivation under C/E. | Deny. Her Coleman join and authored Woodard rule and sufficient-process application support the claim-specific assessments. Historical denial confirms the disposition without importing every historical AEDPA or treaty formulation. No categorical bar to a genuine treaty or judicial-process claim follows. |
| Scalia | Retain T1: receiving-State procedure and the failure to establish objective legal unavailability or an available prejudicial remedy defeat the requested showing; no universal treaty-default rule. | Retain P1: E's permitted collection choice and the present arbitrariness showing do not supply sufficient reversal prospects. C alone creates no mandatory-method entitlement. | Deny. His Coleman/Lonchar joins, Kennedy's Woodard concurrence join and Caspari/Gilmore positions supply the narrow grounds. Historical denial is consistent. He adopts no Claim IV default, universal hearing prohibition or categorical absence of independent constitutional scrutiny. |
| Kennedy | Retain T1: the proviso does not itself overcome the concrete diligence and domestic-relief obstacles for interim review. | Retain P1: the judicial function is materially different from mercy, but neither that distinction nor aggregate counts establishes the claimed federal defect in review actually performed. | Deny. His Coleman join, authored Woodard concurrence and confined Lonchar opportunity join support the result. Historical denial confirms it. No unfinished required judicial opportunity or production duty is invented from uncertainty. |
| Souter | **Revise T2 to denial on an independently sufficient causal/remedial ground.** Even assuming reviewability of the full-effect/default issue, the existing submission does not show a significant possibility that correcting default would overcome the inadequately supported connection between omitted consular advice and conviction or sentence. He reserves the treaty-default merits rather than joining all of T1's reasoning. | **Revise P2 to P1.** Recognize the distinct preserved federal theory, but find insufficient reversal prospects on this submitted comparison-method showing. Correct claim identification does not itself establish an arbitrary substantive deprivation or invalidate the independent merits denial. | **Deny A-732.** His actual historical causal statement is strong evidence on an unchanged material record; his current Woodard sufficient-process join and Coleman independent-barrier framework support the separate process assessment. The reasons and tested possible changed premises are stated below. This is no final prejudice finding, claim-default finding or ruling that all method objections are nonfederal. |
| Thomas | Retain T1: default and distinct relief predicates leave insufficient reversal prospects; notice omission alone does not forbid ordinary diligence requirements. | Retain P1: no sufficient showing of an arbitrary deprivation, and C cannot turn E into an all-records collection command. | Deny. His Coleman/Lonchar joins, Felker statement's independent-relief inquiry, Woodard concurrence join and Caspari/Gilmore joins support these grounds. Historical denial confirms the result without importing chapter 154, an actual §2254(e)(2) failure or Claim IV default. |
| Ginsburg | Retain T2: giving both Article 36(2) clauses their actual operation presents sufficient consequential review prospects; a treaty violation is not itself enforceability or prejudice. | Retain P1: the distinct claim remains recognized, but discretionary accumulation, actual comparison and untested comparability do not independently justify protection. | Grant on the treaty ground only. Her Lindh provision-specific method, Felker, Lonchar and Woodard joins support the limited position. Her historical A-732-specific stay confirms the disposition, without treating first-petition status alone as sufficient or attributing an unwritten Claim IV rationale to her. |
| Breyer | Retain T2: the notice/effective-exercise/default issue and possible legally consequential correction justify preserving review without deciding prejudice. | Retain P1: aggregate outcomes do not establish legally similar crimes and defendants or fundamentally arbitrary adjudication; no independent stay sufficiency. | Grant on the treaty ground only. His Lonchar, Woodard, Felker and Lambrix/O'Dell joins support the limits. His historical dissent directly confirms that novelty, prejudice and nonretroactivity warranted fuller consideration; its possible watershed argument is not a present watershed finding. |

### Souter: tested departure and reconciliation change

The provisional treaty stay treated correction of an arguably mistaken default premise as sufficient despite reserving prejudice. Souter's historical statement expressly identifies a different, independent obstacle: no reasonably arguable causal connection to the conviction or sentence. The neutral record preserves the same noncapital offer, counsel's recommendation, refusal and proposed different effect of consular intervention. It supplies no new advice, communication, supported counterfactual or altered remedy requirement answering that obstacle. The full-effect proviso was in the treaty and in the historical submission; calling attention to it is not a changed premise.

His simulated Coleman dissent supports protection when a potentially erroneous gateway prevents the legally proper inquiry; it does not require protection when an independently sufficient relief obstacle remains. Lonchar protects an identified unfinished legal obligation, which these commitments do not establish. The first-petition posture and A-732-only channel were also present in the historical application; removing Paraguay's separate claims leaves the individual causal ground intact. The operative chapter 153 provisions have separate triggers, so Souter need not adopt the historical per curiam's broad hearing discussion to find this showing inadequate. His support for category-specific Chapman rules in Brecht/O'Neal/Roy does not shift the distinct burden of establishing treaty-related prejudice or establish a consular-error rule.

Accordingly, no concrete changed premise supports retaining T2 for Souter. His reconciled conclusion is a stay-stage insufficiency assessment: possible correction of default does not on this submission establish a significant possibility of a legally consequential reversal past the independent causal/remedial obstacle. It does not declare consular advice universally immaterial, find an undisputed historical fact of no prejudice, or adopt a final rule of individual treaty enforceability.

The process component requires its own assessment. The district's express preservation ruling and the historical petition/reply establish a genuine federal theory. Their recovery cures an operator source gap; it changes neither what the historical application presented nor the statutory terms. ## Judgment and controlling law

The Judgment & Remedy, Opinion Topology and Holdings blocks below are the authoritative component decision and law of this Record. The internal controlling-holding section reproduces the same Holdings text verbatim so its entire rule, authority, explanation and limits pass unchanged to Render Input. The separate Precedent Treatment and Law After Decision blocks perform their own jobs without converting a separate writing into law.

### Controlling holdings (identical public handoff)

### 1. Former-law treatment of the pending capital application

**Holding and operative rule.** The ordinary chapter 153 amendments to §2254(d) and §2254(e)(1)'s replacement factual presumption do not govern this capital habeas application, already pending when AEDPA took effect. Former §2254(d)(8) governs the state-finding inquiry; this construction preserves separately directed provisions and does not establish or dispense with chapter 154's state-qualification conditions.

**Authority.** Stevens's Part I, joined by O'Connor, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer, supplies five votes for the temporal construction. Stone-Zsela supports the operative former-law direction, but not this distinct rationale; Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas reserve the temporal question.

**Controlling explanation.** Lindh v. Murphy, decided June 23, 1997, construed the ordinary chapter 153 amendments by comparing them with Congress's express direction applying chapter 154 to qualifying pending capital cases. Although Lindh's holding involved a noncapital application, the statutory comparison also governs this pending capital application outside any established chapter 154 qualification. Capital status alone does not transform the filing into a post-enactment application or satisfy the separate qualification requirements. No Arizona qualification has been established here. Felker v. Turpin, 518 U.S. 651 (1996), addressed a post-enactment authorization proceeding; its provision-specific result does not make every amended merits or hearing restriction govern an already pending application. The contrary present-authority argument cannot erase the distinctions Congress drew among provisions and regulated proceedings. This holding decides the identified merits and factual-treatment amendments, not every AEDPA provision or future filing. Any genuinely necessary hearing provision retains its own temporal and triggering inquiry; the Court does not decide §2254(e)(2)'s application or order a hearing.

### 2. The gateway requires a whole-record probability determination and a distinct state-finding assessment

**Holding and operative rule.** To pass the innocence gateway for an otherwise barred constitutional claim, reliable new evidence, assessed with the entire probative record, must show that it is more likely than not that no reasonable, properly instructed juror would find guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. The lower court must conduct that inquiry and separately apply former §2254(d)(8); its legally inconsistent analysis cannot sustain the present new-trial instruction, but the Court does not conclusively reject the gateway on this submission.

**Authority.** Stevens's Part II, joined by Stone-Zsela, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer, controls by five votes.

**Additional operative limits.** The State must plead abuse clearly and particularly, identifying prior history and new claims, before the prisoner's responsive burden arises. Former §2244(b)'s refusal permission concerns a prisoner held under a state judgment after a federal court, justice or judge denied release or another habeas remedy following either an evidentiary merits hearing on a material factual issue or a merits hearing on law. Its exception requires both an unadjudicated factual or other ground and satisfaction that the ground was not deliberately withheld or otherwise abusive. When both conditions are met and no other barrier applies, McCleskey requires consideration. New evidence does not necessarily create a new ground. Cause and prejudice, the exceptional innocence route, and independent claim conditions remain distinct. No discretionary refusal may rest on a mistaken gateway standard; gateway passage establishes neither a violation nor automatic relief.

**Controlling explanation.** Schlup v. Delo, decided January 23, 1995, supplies a probability inquiry about reasonable jurors, not the reviewing judge's preferred verdict or confidence in the actual verdict. The en banc opinion recited the correct formula but also used a different confidence inquiry and treated an equally plausible account of Dunbar acting alone as an answer to evidence of joint participation. The required assessment must consider the confession, its later repudiation, the subsequent cellmate account, the corrections information, adverse family accounts, and the disputed tape-fingerprint evidence together. Dunbar's involvement does not itself exclude Carriger's participation. Neither recantation, impeachment, prisoner testimony nor trial inadmissibility categorically removes probative evidence; reliability, timing, motives and corroboration determine its weight.

Former §2254(d) protects a qualifying factual determination made by a competent state court after a merits hearing involving the applicant and the State or its officer or agent, evidenced by adequate written indicia. Paragraph (8) requires consideration of whether the pertinent produced state record as a whole fairly supports the finding. Marshall v. Lonberger, 459 U.S. 422 (1983), supplies the protection for historical and credibility findings; the statute supplies the exception. A plausible different inference, later evidence alone, or the state judge's absence from the original trial does not eliminate that protection. Nor can the prior finding conclusively decide evidence it did not assess. The Court does not find the 1988 credibility determination unsupported.

The argument for immediate gateway rejection gives proper weight to the adverse evidence but does not cure the lower court's failure to perform one consistent legal inquiry on the interdependent record. Meaningful exculpatory evidence remains to be assessed under that inquiry. Remand permits either gateway conclusion and requires no automatic hearing.



### 3. Conditional Brady materiality does not establish suppression or gateway passage

**Holding and operative rule.** If the materially new corrections-file information described by the en banc court is established to have been suppressed under a legally applicable prosecution duty, its collective lawful impeachment, preparation and investigative uses satisfy Brady materiality on this record. A materially smaller proven suppressed set requires its own collective assessment; neither this conditional conclusion nor a successful gateway establishes the other elements of a Brady violation.

**Authority.** Stevens's Part III, joined by Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer, supplies six votes for this conditional instruction. No present Brady violation or entitlement to a writ is adjudicated.

**Controlling explanation.** Kyles v. Whitley, decided April 19, 1995, requires collective consideration of favorable evidence actually suppressed and asks whether its lawful uses create a reasonable probability of a different result. It does not require each item to be independently material, an innocence showing, or a conclusion that acquittal is more likely than conviction. The materially new file information concerns habitual blame shifting, violence and armed conduct contradicting the presentation of the prosecution's central witness. It could affect the framing defense and examination of the investigation, beyond merely adding to the six disclosed burglary convictions and the disclosed gun-form falsehood. The State's reliance on those disclosures, immunity and surviving corroboration does not answer the combined effect of this more specific information.

Suppression remains separate. Knowing that a file exists does not establish knowledge of each favorable item; information actually known to the defense cannot be relabeled suppressed. Carriger's letter directing counsel to obtain the file matters, but does not prove knowledge of every material content. The later confession is not treated as evidence available for trial disclosure years earlier, and speculative investigative fruits are not assumed. Kyles makes knowledge held by police or others acting for this prosecution attributable despite the trial prosecutor's ignorance; it does not impute every government repository's contents. Actual case-team knowledge remains unresolved here. Once a complete Brady violation is established, Kyles requires no second duplicative harmlessness inquiry. Brecht and Roy supply no general alternative prejudice screen overriding that incorporated materiality rule.

### 4. The mandate preserves the bounded acquisition question without deciding it

**Holding and operative rule.** After the required gateway analysis, the lower courts must decide the Brady claim if the gateway or an independent lawful route permits merits review. Actual case-team attribution and the proposed duty to obtain the State's identified corrections file on its own central witness remain distinct available theories; the mandate neither makes proof of actual team possession the exclusive route nor adopts the proposed acquisition duty.

**Authority.** Stevens's Part IV, joined by Stone-Zsela, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer, controls the remand by five votes.

**Controlling explanation.** Kyles's affirmative responsibility for information held by the prosecution team can resolve suppression if the requisite facts are established. Its organizational boundary does not itself decide whether the State's choice to rely on this known central witness requires obtaining the identified credibility file from corrections officials. That proposed duty has a specific fair-trial basis and raises a distinct objection concerning acquisition of information from a separate repository. It is neither equivalent to universal government imputation nor established simply because the file would be useful or accessible.

If actual attribution is absent or insufficient and the acquisition theory remains necessary and properly presented through a lawful merits route, its constitutional merits and any actually applicable collateral conditions must be considered. The remand does not require extra fact development solely to avoid an otherwise properly decidable legal question. Unknown presentation, finality or waiver facts establish no Teague defense and impose no duty on Carriger to disprove an unasserted bar. An extension beyond Kyles's precise holding is not automatically a new rule under Teague. If nonretroactivity is properly available, the finality-era dictated-rule inquiry and both contemporary exceptions—substantive restrictions on punishment and watershed procedures essential to accuracy and fundamental fairness—retain their own requirements. No such classification or exception is decided here.

The Court awards no freestanding innocence relief and sets no uniform standard for that claim. Herrera v. Collins, 506 U.S. 390 (1993), supplies only its record-specific insufficiency holding. If the gateway fails and no independent lawful route exists, the Brady claim supplies no writ. If a lawful route and a complete conviction-level Brady violation are established, conditional new-trial relief remains available under the governing habeas rules. No outcome, hearing or retrial period is predetermined.

**Frozen sources.** The [resumed commitments](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK6_RESUMED_COMMITMENTS.md), including the [acquisition clarification](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK6_RESUMED_CARRIGER_ACQUISITION_CHECK.md), and [final reconciliation, §5](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK6_RESUMED_RECONCILED.md#5-carriger-v-stewart--april-16-1998) remain unchanged. Isolated neutral/model/reconciliation stages are reused; the present context is assembly and makes no claim to Stone blindness.

| Stevens | Authored Schlup supports correcting the mixed probability analysis; Kyles join supports conditional materiality; Lindh join supports the bounded statutory extension. No present gateway success or definitive failure; acquisition reserved. | Authors and joins I–IV; the mandate requires the exact correction and leaves both merits routes available. No changed commitment. |
| O'Connor | Schlup join fixes the actual burden; Herrera and Felker support record-specific failure despite meaningful impeachment. Lindh and Kyles joins support transition and conditional materiality independently. | Joins I and III only; dissents from renewed gateway review in II and IV. Personal ignorance and knowledge of a file's existence do not settle suppression. No changed commitment. |
| Scalia | Felker supports failure under governing Schlup despite his earlier dissent; Lindh dissent makes temporal reservation appropriate where former-law failure suffices. Kyles governs without supplying an acquisition answer. | Joins O'Connor's dissent only; agrees to remove the writ instruction and preserve independent claims. Does not adopt transition or conditional materiality; no stricter burden or categorical recantation rule. No changed commitment. |
| Kennedy | Authored Schlup dissent and later Felker join support testing Carriger's participation, while governing Schlup controls the burden. Herrera concurrence and Kyles dissent do not resolve acquisition. | Joins O'Connor's dissent only on correct-standard failure; reserves transition and materiality and makes no conclusive tape or possession finding. No changed commitment. |
| Souter | Schlup join supports a correction rather than treating surviving adverse evidence as conclusive; authored Kyles requires genuine suppression while allowing collective lawful uses. Lindh join supplies transition. | Joins I–IV; no exclusive actual-possession route and no premature acquisition ruling. No changed commitment. |
| Thomas | Felker's provision/activity method supports reserving unnecessary transition; current Schlup rather than his preferred stricter/refusal theories supplies the gateway result. | Joins O'Connor's dissent only; no invented withholding, discovery obligation, automatic writ or anti-acquisition holding. No changed commitment. |
| Ginsburg | Authored Lindh supports the limited capital extension; full Schlup and Kyles joins require separate state-finding, gateway and materiality inquiries. | Joins I–IV; no blanket AEDPA exemption, assumed chapter 154 qualification or unsupported credibility finding. No changed commitment. |
| Breyer | Schlup, Kyles, Lindh and Felker joins support corrective review without automatic fact development or eventual relief. | Joins I–IV; no invented investigative fruit or retrospective availability of the later confession. No changed commitment. |

The exact four-part compatibility preserves each recorded objection rather than revising a commitment. All eight continue to reserve the bounded acquisition duty's constitutional merits. The four remanding Associates accept Part IV because it requires the correct gateway inquiry and preserves both actual attribution and acquisition if needed; the other four still require rejection of this gateway. Stone's new operative vote makes the former a majority without purporting to answer the latter's evidentiary objection. Agreement on vacatur alone is not counted as agreement on the complete remand. No revised non-Stone commitment or new reconciliation is required.

**Historical reconciliation.** Carriger has no historical Supreme Court merits alignment in the authorized comparator. Neither the lower majority and dissent nor historical petition treatment supplies Associate votes, authorship or a Court holding. The final frozen reconciliation made no Carriger departure. No Historical departure or Consequence label is warranted: no merits comparator is displaced and no predicate of an identified later historical matter is expressly displaced by this decision.

**Published noncontrolling continuity.** Stone's concurrence retains the bounded readily-accessible DOC-file duty, its gateway/materiality application and his preferred conditional new-trial remedy; it is not an acquired Court holding. O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas retain their submission-specific gateway failure assessment and preference to limit further proceedings to independent claims; they reserve acquisition and do not foreclose genuinely new lawful routes. O'Connor's joins in the temporal and conditional-materiality holdings are controlling at those levels and are not attributed to her three dissent joiners. **Procedure and dependencies.** There is no roster, participation, circuit or standing-practice change. Lower-court proceedings follow the mandate; no new Supreme Court date or event is created. ## Decision kernel, participation and entering law

This is the authorized plenary review under 28 U.S.C. §1254(1) of the Sixth Circuit’s final injunction judgment, 130 F.3d 187, entered November 18, 1997. April 20, 1998 is the existing authorized event date; no new grant, argument, submission date or Supreme Court docket is inferred. The district court’s preliminary injunction became permanent on January 12, 1996 after the parties stipulated to consolidation with trial. The Sixth Circuit sustained whole-Act relief. ## Decision kernel and entering law

The event date and argument date are supported by the frozen neutral packet's published procedural account. The question is whether Treasury's treatment of reserve strengthening in the transition to discounted insurance-loss reserves is consistent with the Tax Reform Act of 1986. The question is an analytical formulation, not an asserted verbatim petition quotation. All nine seated Justices participate at argument and decision; the quorum is satisfied and five votes are required. No material jurisdictional or preservation barrier appears in the frozen record.

The material facts are the reported $519,987 deficiency attributable to net additions to the 1986 reserves and the undisputed absence of a change in computational methods or assumptions. The exact entering-law slice is [Atlantic entering law](../entering-law/OT_1997CHUNK7_A_ATLANTIC.md). Hill separates legal tax categories from commercial aggregation. assignment_statements.text:
**Case and dockets:** Campbell v. Louisiana, No. 96-1584.
**Event and date:** Threshold decision after plenary review, 1998-04-21; October Term 1997, chunk 7.
**Result:** Louisiana Supreme Court reversed and remanded, 9–0; personal due-process standing is unanimous; third-party equal-protection standing has six votes.

## Decision kernel and entering law

On certiorari to the Court of Appeal of Louisiana, Third Circuit, 673 So. 2d 1061, after the Louisiana Supreme Court refused to reconsider the grand-jury issue, 685 So. 2d 140, following its standing decision at 661 So. 2d 1321. Argued January 20, 1998; decided April 21, 1998, on the published chronology preserved in the frozen neutral packet. The question is whether a white defendant may challenge alleged racial discrimination against Black persons in choosing the grand-jury foreperson. All nine Justices participate at argument and decision; quorum exists and five votes suffice. The standing question is adjudicated, not the discrimination merits. This threshold character excludes the signed opinion from subsequent plenary-merits assignment counts.

Campbell filed a timely pretrial challenge. The reported evidence was no Black foreperson from January 1976 through August 1993 despite registered voters being more than twenty percent Black; the State did not dispute that account. The Court of Appeal considered the proof inadequate and contemplated an evidentiary hearing. Those are recitations and lower-court assessments, not a finding of discriminatory purpose here. Louisiana chooses the foreperson from the venire before drawing the remaining members by lot, and the foreperson has a full vote. The published procedural account also supplies the specific absence of established appellate presentation of the Sixth Amendment claim. Missing archived original filings establish no independent default.

The [entering-law slice](../entering-law/OT_1997CHUNK7_A_CAMPBELL.md) supplies McCollum and J.E.B., including their distinct attribution, juror-right, proof and remedy rules and the prior published positions of O'Connor, Kennedy, Scalia and Thomas. Powers remains the governing third-party-standing framework. Hobby concerns appointment from an already constituted federal grand jury. No completed intervening April 20 law displaces these premises; the April 21 peers supply no entering law to one another. Research cutoff: April 21, 1998. Full original petitions, merits briefs and appendices were not independently recovered in preflight; the supported record suffices for this threshold decision without a new factual premise.

## Stone and final compatibility

The [per-case Stone supplement](../runtime/OT_1997CHUNK7_A_CAMPBELL_STONE.md) directs reversal and remand on Campbell's own due-process standing. His approved ground is personal subjection to the charging authority of an allegedly race-composed grand jury, redressable by lawful correction; Hobby differs because Louisiana selects a voting member before completing the body. Stone expressly does not reach third-party equal protection, the unpreserved Sixth Amendment theory or discrimination merits. He defines no substantive due-process rule and prescribes no relief after a proved violation.

Stone joins Part II's personal-standing ground and Part III's preservation and bounded common remand. He joins no Part I third-party-standing proposition and neither adopts nor dissents from that additional route. His concurrence explains why the direct route suffices and why he does not reach the other. This separate writing performs legal work by distinguishing nonreach from Scalia and Thomas's substantive rejection of third-party standing. It adds no ground. No fallback is used and no opinion join depends on omitted choices.

## Form, assignment and joins

Before any count, one signed opinion is appropriate for the two independently sufficient standing routes and the common reservation/remand. Part I recognizes the excluded jurors' equal-protection route; Part II recognizes Campbell's own due-process route; Part III states preservation and the common limits on further proceedings. All nine support reversal and remand on Part II. Six Associates support every proposition; Scalia and Thomas refuse Part I, and Stone does not reach it. The Chief assigns from the common judgment coalition. Fresh actual-Record recount: Stone-Zsela 6; Stevens 7; O'Connor 7; Scalia 6; Kennedy 7; Souter 7; Thomas 6; Ginsburg 7; Breyer 6. Complete-opinion eligible authors: Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer. Lowest eligible count: 6. Pool: all six, at 6 or 7. Chosen author: Breyer. The legal work is to apply Powers' three requirements to direct judicial selection, distinguish a full member from an officer chosen later, and keep threshold access separate from proof and relief. His frozen complete formulation carries those distinctions without a new accommodation and without attributing J.E.B. participation to him. Kennedy is the strongest alternative because his individual-citizen explanation precisely preserves the group-representation limit. Breyer can incorporate that already shared formulation equally faithfully and has the lower count. No unresolved objection calls for expansion authorship. Stone cannot write the complete opinion because his approved position does not reach Part I; his direct-route preference supplies no full-opinion eligibility. One author can carry all parts, so divided authorship is unnecessary.

Final compatibility: Breyer, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter and Ginsburg join all parts. Stone, Scalia and Thomas join Parts II and III. Scalia writes the shared concurrence in part and dissent in part, joined by Thomas; this selection reflects their shared Powers objection preserved in Scalia's J.E.B. dissent, not historical current-case authorship. Stone separately concurs in part and in the judgment. No commitment changes or invented draft exchanges are needed. Parts II and III have nine direct joins; Part I has six. No Marks synthesis applies.

Campbell may pursue both routes established by the Court, with standing distinguished from success. State evidentiary and merits proceedings remain open under the remand; no later outcome is presumed.

assignment_statements.text:
**Case and dockets:** California v. Deep Sea Research, Inc., No. 96-1400.
**Event and date:** Plenary merits decision, 1998-04-22; October Term 1997, chunk 7.
**Result:** Affirmed in part, vacated in part and remanded, 9–0; in-rem jurisdiction sustained, premature ASA and title-related conclusions vacated.
**Version / lineage:** Original decision in this run; supersedes no completed adjudication.

## Decision kernel and entering law

Certiorari to the Ninth Circuit, 102 F.3d 379, reviewing the district court's orders reported at 883 F. Supp. 1343. Argued December 1, 1997; decided April 22, 1998, on the published chronology in the neutral packet. The question concerns California's claimed Eleventh Amendment immunity in a federal admiralty in-rem proceeding involving a wreck the State does not possess. The opinion also determines the governing source and limits of the ASA inquiry and vacates premature ownership-related conclusions. All nine Justices participate at both milestones; quorum exists and five votes suffice. The limited State appearance is not consent or waiver. This signed plenary decision includes substantive statutory construction and title-remand instructions and is counted once under §8.

The Brother Jonathan sank in 1865. California neither located nor possessed it. DSR began this action in 1991, located the wreck in 1994, recovered artifacts and acquired some insurers' subrogation interests. It stipulated for the pending motions to location on California submerged lands. The district court appointed it custodian and exclusive salvor but deferred final title and distribution and did not determine individual cargo status. The United States later asserted its own property claim. These published recitations do not establish abandonment, embeddedness, National Register eligibility or ownership of all portions. No new accounting, location or title fact is inferred. Full original briefs and appendix were not independently recovered in preflight; that limit establishes no missing court papers, default or failure of proof.

The [entering-law slice](../entering-law/OT_1997CHUNK7_A_DEEP_SEA.md) preserves Coeur d'Alene's prospective-officer route and its prohibition on binding an immune State's title in that action, along with Seminole's actual officer holding and absence of a controlling direct-State constitutional rationale. Those rules do not decide this traditional maritime res proceeding. The Davis and Ex parte New York (No. 2) supply the actual-possession distinction. The neutral packet contains complete §§2105–2106 terms. Atlantic's tax construction, Beach's rescission expiration and Campbell's criminal-jury standing decision, all April 21, alter no relevant immunity, maritime title or ASA premise. No completed April 20 rule is material, and same-day Miller supplies no entering law. Research cutoff: April 22, 1998.

## Stone and final compatibility

The [per-case Stone supplement](../runtime/OT_1997CHUNK7_A_DEEP_SEA_STONE.md) directs affirmance of jurisdiction, vacatur of premature ASA/title conclusions and remand. His approved ground separates federal arrest of an unpossessed res from compulsion of a State or seizure of State-held property. The title assertion establishes neither immunity nor ownership. Abandonment, statutory coverage, title and salvage require independent source-specific adjudication; no personal/treasury relief or State-held-property rule follows.

Stone joins Parts I and II on immunity and binding adjudication of the competing interests, and Part IV's complete disposition and reservations. He also agrees that the ASA inquiry remains for the remand. He does not join Part III's additional construction of maritime abandonment through express or inferred renunciation and its associated categorical-evidence restrictions; his approved source-specific remand does not independently supply those interpretive propositions. This is a scope limit, not a contrary abandonment rule. No fallback, new ground, altered remedy or separate Stone writing is used; the stated joins represent his approved public position.

## Form, assignment and final joins

Before counting, the legal work requires one signed opinion after plenary review. Parts I–II state the traditional immunity boundary and its binding in-rem consequence; Part III supplies the separate ASA source, conditions and construction; Part IV gives the mixed disposition and bounded remand. These are substantive distinctions, not count-driven divisions. All nine support each formal judgment component. All eight Associates join the full governing rationale; Stone's stated scope does not include every Part III proposition.

The Chief assigns. Fresh actual-Record recount before assignment: Stone-Zsela 6; Stevens 7; O'Connor 7; Scalia 6; Kennedy 7; Souter 7; Thomas 6; Ginsburg 7; Breyer 6. Counted opinions: 59. Last counted: Beach v. Ocwen Federal Bank, April 21, 1998. Campbell is a threshold standing decision and is excluded, as are the other procedural/threshold actions, summaries, per curiams, separate writings and Section 10 explanations. Actual opinion tables, including the earlier records in this Run, control rather than prior assignment totals.

Eligible complete-opinion authors: Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. Minimum eligible count: 6. Pool: all eight, at 6 or 7. Chosen author: Scalia. His frozen position expressly distinguishes the surviving traditional maritime rule from his broader constitutional immunity position, and separately rejects treating jurisdiction as ownership or congressional abrogation. That formulation directly addresses the opinion's principal risk of collapsing different lawful routes. Breyer is the strongest equal-count alternative for preserving the individual property questions and avoiding administrability as an ownership premise; Scalia's explicit separation of the immunity domains better fits the lead holding while carrying the agreed title limits. Thomas is also fully eligible, without any capability exclusion. No additional agreement is needed from a conditional Justice, so expansion supplies no separate preference. Stone is not eligible for the complete opinion because his approved remand does not supply every Part III interpretation; division among authors is unnecessary because one eligible author carries all parts.

All eight Associates join Parts I–IV; Stone joins I–II and IV. Stevens files his additional broader admiralty explanation. Kennedy authors the shared reservation joined by Ginsburg and Breyer; Kennedy's frozen position identifies why the nonpossession holding need not settle the future State-possession case, and those two expressly share that ground. Authorship is selected here, not copied from historical lineup. These writings fully join the Court at their stated scope. No Associate commitment changes after reconciliation, no invented circulation history is used, and every holding has a direct majority.

## Adaptive audit annex

Frozen inputs: [neutral packet](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK7_A_DEEP_SEA_NEUTRAL.md), [commitments](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK7_A_DEEP_SEA_COMMITMENTS.md), [reconciliation](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK7_A_DEEP_SEA_RECONCILED.md). Independent modeling and historical reconciliation were separate Stone-free contexts. Reconciliation read the full main opinion, both concurrences and footnotes. It clarified the form of relief from unqualified vacatur to affirming jurisdiction and vacating the remainder, preserving all provisional substantive positions, and restored the substantive separate-writing functions. No material new neutral premise was added.

| Justice | Frozen final judgment and rationale | Specific historical comparison and barriers |
|---|---|---|
| Stevens | Affirm jurisdiction, vacate remainder, remand; complete opinion plus broader concurrence | Historical match. The Davis and his Seminole/Coeur positions support the route; his broader maritime view is separate, not controlling. |
| O'Connor | Same; complete opinion | Historical match. Her Coeur objection concerned practical displacement of actual sovereign control, absent for this never-possessed wreck. No all-admiralty exception. |
| Scalia | Same; complete opinion | Historical match. The traditional maritime distinction coexists with his Seminole immunity position; no abrogation or ownership ruling. |
| Kennedy | Same; complete opinion plus shared reservation | Historical match. Coeur's exercised-control concern does not immunize bare title; future possessed-property question remains open. |
| Souter | Same; complete opinion | Historical match. The Davis suffices without adopting his conditional Seminole theories or imposing a claim-proof burden before immunity. |
| Thomas | Same; complete opinion | Historical match. His Seminole/Coeur commitments preserve immunity in its actual domain without immunizing every ownership assertion. |
| Ginsburg | Same; complete opinion and Kennedy concurrence | Historical match. Her Coeur/Seminole positions separate jurisdiction, title and relief; broader possession question reserved. |
| Breyer | Same; complete opinion and Kennedy concurrence | Historical match. The route permits actual title adjudication; convenience does not establish unitary cargo status. |

The historical sufficient nonpossession ground survives unchanged. No material historical departure is asserted. Coeur d'Alene's ban on binding an immune State's title in an officer suit is not imported into this different rule permitting binding in-rem adjudication. The strongest contrary immunity argument points to that binding effect, but fails to justify discarding the actual-possession distinction in the maritime precedents. The contrary overbroad argument that an in-rem caption defeats all immunity and gives DSR title is likewise rejected. No colorable-title proof burden, final abandonment finding, completed salvage entitlement or broad §6313 preemption holding is adopted.

## Continuity and validation

The district court retains jurisdiction for independent title and ASA proceedings. No ownership, distribution or salvage outcome is presumed. Stevens's noncontrolling concurrence questions importing officer-possession limits into the distinctive maritime res proceeding; Kennedy, Ginsburg and Breyer preserve reconsideration of the constitutional possession distinction in a future case while fully supporting this one. No procedural institution, roster or broader immunity regime changes.

Checked: lawful certiorari posture, chronology/intervening law, nine participants, unanimous mixed remedy, eight full versus Stone's partial rationale joins, every ASA category/qualification/transition, no waiver inference, binding in-rem effect, balanced assignment from actual tables, frozen separate-writing scope, Stone fixed core and public/private boundary. Structural and explanation-ceiling results are in the chunk assembly QA receipt. Parent term-wide integration checks remain separate and are not claimed complete here. No unresolved substantive blocker. Durable record: this file.

assignment_statements.text:
**Case and dockets:** Chaudhuri v. Tennessee; Sixth Circuit No. 96-5538; no separate Supreme Court docket supplied.
**Event and date:** Merits decision; 1998-04-27 (OT1997, chunk 7).
**Result:** Affirmed as to genuine moments of silence, 9–0; reversed as to officially arranged spoken prayers, 6–3; remanded within the questions reviewed.
**Version / lineage:** Original decision.

## Event, entering law and scope

The April 27 date is the authorized scheduling premise for review under 28 U.S.C. §1254(1) of the Sixth Circuit’s November 18, 1997 judgment, 130 F.3d 232. No argument date, historical grant or separate Supreme Court number is reconstructed. The sitting nine participate at submission and decision; no nonparticipation is established. The granted questions concern official university invocations, including benedictions within the same former practice, and genuine designated silence. Private audience recitations, Title VII and unrelated claims remain outside review.

The entering-law slice `../entering-law/OT_1997CHUNK7_chaudhuri.md` supplies Agostini’s updated single Lemon inquiry, Tanford’s December 22 official-university-worship rule, Sherman’s civic distinction, Lee and Ingebretsen’s independent sponsorship and pressure grounds, and Arizonans’s continuing-controversy limits. The prayer holding extends Tanford’s operative official-worship principle from commencement to the other university functions actually containing the same officially arranged practice; it does not decide all adult ceremonial arrangements. The silence question reserved by Tanford is resolved on its actual operation here.

## Stone and final compatibility

The approved case-specific supplement `../runtime/OT_1997CHUNK7_B_CHAUDHURI_STONE.md` supplies partial reversal and affirmance, the official/private boundary, the updated Lemon method, and ordinary remand. Stone joins both parts in full. His acceptance of the surviving damages controversy does not adjudge the named administrators’ capacities, a cause of action, immunity or damages. The supported live claim, rather than a damages demand against the State alone, permits review. The prospective controversy remains for ordinary consideration. No standing fallback, new ground, substantive narrowing or modified remedy is used. The separate practical-pressure ground is not reached by the Court.

## Frozen commitments and reconciliation audit

Authoritative handoffs: `../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK7_B_CHAUDHURI_COMMITMENTS.md`, the independent `../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK7_B_CHAUDHURI_MODEL_CLARIFICATION.md`, and `../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK7_B_CHAUDHURI_RECONCILED.md`. The clarification replaces only the unsupported operator-gap inference with the lower opinion’s affirmative damages-liveness account. All eight Associates support review of that live controversy, preservation of remaining defenses, and affirmance of the actual silence ruling.

| Justice | Frozen sufficient ground and final scope |
|---|---|
| Stevens | Sherman civic-function join permits this silence; Lee, Ingebretsen and Tanford joins require prayer reversal. Arizonans supplies no invented jurisdictional defect. Full join. |
| O'Connor | Sherman and her Wallace silence distinction permit nondevotional reflection; Agostini and Tanford govern official prayer. Full join without freestanding Lemon prongs. |
| Scalia | Sherman and Agostini permit the actual silence; Tanford dissent retains voluntary adult ceremonial permission and his compulsion account. Part I only; dissents from prayer reversal. |
| Kennedy | Sherman permits silence; Tanford dissent retains adult ceremonial permission. Lee and Ingebretsen preserve practical pressure, but the nonmonitoring/no-penalty evidence and dean’s affidavit do not establish it here. Part I only; dissent retains a standard not requiring formal punishment. |
| Souter | Sherman distinguishes actual civic reflection; Lee, Ingebretsen and Tanford forbid officially arranged worship. Full join; a silence label cannot immunize directed devotion. |
| Thomas | Sherman’s concrete civic ground and Agostini permit silence; Tanford dissent supplies adult ceremonial permission and compulsion account. Part I only; dissents from prayer reversal. |
| Ginsburg | Sherman permits the actual silence; her Ingebretsen opinion and Tanford join forbid official prayer. Full join; conceded lack of complicity bars attributing the audience recitations to the university. |
| Breyer | Sherman, Ingebretsen and Tanford supply the same distinction. Full join without a new pressure finding or immunity determination. |

There is no historical Supreme Court merits comparator. Lower Judges’ positions supply no Supreme Court vote. The change from the Sixth Circuit’s prayer judgment follows current Agostini and intervening Tanford. No material historical-departure label is warranted. The majority rejects adult voluntariness as a cure for government worship; the dissent preserves that actual doctrinal disagreement. The majority does not require the dissenters to surrender their pressure and compulsion distinctions to join silence.

## Sources, cutoff and continuity

Research cutoff: April 27, 1998. The frozen neutral packet and `../research/chunk7_neutral_b/SUPPLEMENT.md` use the full lower opinion at 130 F.3d 232, including paragraphs 22, 34, 47 and Jones’s separate writing. Paragraph 22 supports a live damages controversy, while only tentatively describing prospective mootness. The complaint, capacities, statutory damages basis and immunity ruling are not represented as recovered. These limits justify reserving remedies, not a production order or an invented litigation default. The source supplement’s earlier tentative threshold fork is governed by the frozen clarification and reconciliation.

The Court’s holding governs official prayer at the supported functions and genuine silence. Scalia and Thomas retain a noncontrolling voluntary-adult-ceremony/compulsion position; Kennedy retains a noncontrolling practical-pressure analysis under Lee, without requiring formal penalties. No roster, allotment, new application, automatic hearing or external follow-on event arises.

## Current-law refresh

The exact April 21–22 Public Projections in `../entering-law/OT_1997CHUNK7_B_CURRENT_PUBLIC.md` were screened before assembly. Atlantic Mutual’s reserve-transition construction, Beach’s specific rescission expiration and exception, and Campbell’s separate standing routes change no predicate here. Deep Sea Research concerns the unpossessed maritime res and its source-specific title/remedy inquiry; it supplies no general sovereign-immunity or remedial rule altering this case. Miller establishes the bounded permission to present the father’s claim but no controlling equality, citizenship-remedy or general reopening rule. Neither changes this case’s claimant, scope, governing doctrine or approved Stone position. No earlier B event precedes this decision.

## Assignment

**Form decided before counting:** One signed merits opinion, with a common threshold-and-silence part and a six-Justice official-prayer part. Both questions arise from the same university program and lower judgment; the different joins require parts, not different lead authors. The opinion applies the updated Lemon inquiry, permits genuine silence, and applies the official-worship prohibition to the university’s arranged prayers. Ordinary remand preserves independent liability and relief questions.

**Assignment authority:** The Chief Justice is in the tentative judgment coalition and assigns. Agreement on the entire proposed rationale, rather than judgment alone, establishes eligibility.

|---|---:|
| Stone-Zsela | 6 |
| Stevens | 8 |
| O'Connor | 7 |

**Last event counted:** Miller v. Albright, No. 96-1060.; 1998-04-22.

**Balance pool:** Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer; eligible minimum 6, ceiling 7.

**Author selected:** Breyer. Fit governs because the frozen coalition already shares the complete functional distinction and no necessary join requires new accommodation. Breyer can state the concrete difference between nondevotional silence and officially organized prayer while keeping the supported record and remedial reservations separate. His Sherman, Ingebretsen and Tanford joins support precisely that task. O'Connor brings her Sherman authorship but has the higher count. Stone is the strongest equal-count alternative through his Tanford opinion, yet extending its settled official-worship boundary and deciding this actual silence practice requires no new formulation he uniquely supplies. Breyer can carry that objective equally well; there is no concrete self-assignment advantage. The dissent authorship follows the recorded distinct grounds and does not enter the balance count.

The count was recomputed from actual current-term opinion tables immediately before writing this Record. Separates, per curiam, threshold, summary and other procedural actions do not count. Each signed plenary lead author counts once. No commitment changed in circulation and no invented draft history supplies a join.

## Validation and durable status

Assembled from the frozen neutral and reconciled handoffs and the approved case-specific Stone supplement. The nine participants provide a quorum; five votes suffice. Final component votes and exact joins were checked against those handoffs, with the limits below preserved. The controlling propositions and complete operative remedy are stated in the bounded Public Projection; no separate internal rule changes them. Source cutoffs and independent-stage limits are retained in the audit. All eleven public blocks occur once in contract order, and each ordinary controlling explanation is within 350 words.
