**Case and dockets:** Edwards v. United States; No. 96-8732.
**Event and date:** Merits decision; 1998-04-28 (OT1997, chunk 7).
**Result:** Seventh Circuit judgment affirmed, 9–0, on the bounded Guidelines question.
**Version / lineage:** Original decision.

## Event, entering law and scope

No. 96-8732 was argued February 23 and is decided April 28, 1998, on review under §1254(1) of the Seventh Circuit sentencing judgment. All nine sitting Justices participate at argument and decision. The question is whether the alternative cocaine-or-cocaine-base instruction and general guilty verdict categorically prevent the sentencing judge’s cocaine and crack findings. The Court reaches that question and no universal drug-element classification.

`../entering-law/OT_1997CHUNK7_edwards.md` supplies Witte’s distinction between relevant-conduct use and independent punishment, Watts’s bounded ordinary-sentencing permission, Gaudin’s actual-element allocation, Johnson’s distinct forfeiture framework, and the March 24 Almendarez-Torres statutory element decision. The latter does not announce a universal constitutional rule; this case needs no greater ceiling than the cocaine-only conviction supports. Rogers supplies no omitted-element harmless-error holding. No same-term decision displaces the supported ceiling or same-course predicates.

## Stone and final compatibility

The approved `../runtime/OT_1997CHUNK7_B_EDWARDS_STONE.md` supports affirmance conditional on each sentence remaining within the statutory range supported by the conviction. The frozen objective supplement expressly establishes, as a supported published recitation, that every sentence meets the cocaine-only limits given the quantities attributed to that defendant. That satisfies the condition without inventing sentence amounts or claiming independent examination of an unavailable appendix. Stone joins the entire opinion; no standing fallback, additional ground or discretionary substantive revision is used. The opinion does not say Guidelines findings enlarge the conviction or that every sentencing fact is an element.

## Frozen commitments and reconciliation audit

Sources: `../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK7_B_EDWARDS_COMMITMENTS.md` and `../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK7_B_EDWARDS_RECONCILED.md`. All eight Associates affirm and join the same bounded rule.

| Justice | Sufficient ground and retained limit |
|---|---|
| Stevens | Same-course conduct supports the range even assuming cocaine-only guilt; Gaudin and his Almendarez-Torres join preserve elements and ceilings. His Witte dissent and Watts nonjoin are not converted into broader acquitted-conduct agreement. |
| O'Connor | Her Witte opinion and Watts join support ordinary findings within conviction authority; Gaudin preserves elements. Her Almendarez-Torres recidivism dissent does not alter this case. |
| Scalia | Watts permits ordinary findings; Gaudin and Almendarez-Torres distinguish punishment authority from range selection. No claim that drug kind or amount is always a sentencing factor is adopted. |
| Kennedy | Witte and Gaudin permit this single prosecution’s bounded findings; no new Watts acquitted-conduct join or enlarged recidivism rule follows. |
| Souter | Witte, Watts, Gaudin and Almendarez-Torres support the same ceiling/element distinction; drug-element classification remains open. |
| Thomas | Watts and Gaudin support conduct selection. His Witte judgment-only ground and recidivism dissent remain distinct. |
| Ginsburg | Witte, Watts, Gaudin and her Almendarez-Torres join require supported conduct and lawful punishment authority, not a universal below-maximum safe harbor. |
| Breyer | Witte and Watts support the Guidelines allocation; Gaudin preserves elements. His recidivism dissent does not support exceeding the cocaine-only ceiling. |

Historical unanimity confirms these commitments on the unchanged same-course and cocaine-only-ceiling premises. No material historical departure occurs; historical authorship is not adopted. The strongest contrary theory would make the verdict’s cocaine-only assumption categorically defeat crack consideration. It fails because the same relevant-conduct range follows even on that assumption. A distinct factual, proof, statutory-maximum or element objection is not disposed of merely by labeling the finding sentencing-related. No commitment changed during assembly.

## Sources, cutoff and continuity

Research cutoff: April 28, 1998. The frozen neutral packet’s objective record supplement, neutral-preflight supplement and reconciled review identify the published account at 523 U.S. 511. The full substantive Cornell opinion and complete syllabus were reviewed in reconciliation; the opinion page’s missing terminal words do not obscure the syllabus’s express disposition. The published ceiling account cites the Government brief at 15–16 and notes 6–7 and appendix pages 42–47, 72–82, 107–112, 136–141 and 163–169. ## Event, entering law and scope

| Souter | Discovery Network, Ladue and McIntyre support the concrete line; no invented inadequate-channel finding. |
| Thomas | Ward and his Ladue join support these fully protected activities; his McIntyre ground protects individual communication. This is not a retroactive join in Discovery Network’s commercial-speech rationale. |

No Supreme Court merits comparator exists; the Ninth Circuit’s panel authorship supplies no Justice vote. The trial findings that these plaintiffs’ goods are integrated with protected messages defeat that proxy here. assignment_statements.text:
**Case and dockets:** Ricci v. Village of Arlington Heights; No. 97-501.
**Event and date:** Merits decision; 1998-05-04 (OT1997, chunk 7).
**Result:** Targeted reversal and remand, 5–4; adverse summary judgment on the preserved custody-reasonableness claim set aside. No controlling conclusion on this custody’s ultimate reasonableness.
**Version / lineage:** Original decision.

## Event, entering law and scope

No. 97-501 was argued April 21 and is decided May 4, 1998. All nine participate at argument and decision. Review under §1254(1) concerns the Seventh Circuit’s June 20, 1997 affirmance of summary judgment, 116 F.3d 288, No. 96-2229. Probable cause and local arrest authority are accepted; the preserved question is the objective reasonableness of automatic station-house custody for the fine-only civil business-license violation. The warrant-clause theory first advanced at appellate argument was held waived, and Ricci conceded an arrest under a warrant would be reasonable. No search or no-probable-cause claim is revived. Same-day Perry supplies no entering law.

`../entering-law/OT_1997CHUNK7_ricci.md` and the frozen additional neutral review supply Whren’s bounded initial-stop rule, Robinette’s independent later-restraint inquiry, Ayeni’s purpose-bound execution rule, Wilson’s historical reasonableness method, Soldal’s civil coverage/violation distinction and Lanier’s conduct-time clarity rule. This decision adds a bounded application to fine-only licensing custody, not a preexisting categorical arrest prohibition or a finding that every arrest requires the least restrictive alternative.

## Stone and final compatibility

`../runtime/OT_1997CHUNK7_B_RICCI_STONE.md` approves reversal insofar as summary judgment rests on categorical validity of the automatic policy, with remand for policy causation, preserved defenses and relief. It separately concludes the actual custody lacked a sufficient enforcement connection. Stone supports Part I and the targeted reversal/remand judgment, states his stronger actual-unreasonableness conclusion separately, and does not join Part II’s affirmative reservation of that application. His remand position is narrower than the four-Justice lead explanation: he would leave only remaining liability, defenses and relief. The Court’s absence of a controlling application conclusion does not erase his own conclusion or make him an advocate of leaving it undecided. No standing fallback, new Stone ground, forced full join or narrowing of his fixed core is used.

## Frozen commitments and scoped circulation audit

The original `../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK7_B_RICCI_COMMITMENTS.md` and `../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK7_B_RICCI_RECONCILED.md` remain intact. Four Associates originally selected vacatur/remand and four affirmance. Assembly did not relabel that 4/1/4 disposition split as a uniform majority. The sanitized proposed public ground was returned to a context receiving no Stone supplement. Its authoritative response is `../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK7_B_RICCI_CIRCULATION_AUDIT.md`.

| Justice | Frozen position and date-eligible basis | Audited accommodation and final scope |
|---|---|---|
| Stevens | Vacate because the categorical rule foreclosed actual review; Robinette dissent and Whren/Wilson/Ayeni joins preserve added-restraint limits. | Accepts targeted reversal of the categorical ground and resulting summary judgment, with actual reasonableness expressly unresolved in his rationale. Wilson and his Soldal join support this remedial form. Joins Parts I–II. |
| O'Connor | Vacate for objective enforcement assessment, without universal citation, least restrictive means or premature immunity rejection; Robinette opinion and Ayeni merits join. | Accepts targeted reversal because nonexclusive practical justifications, open application and conduct-time defenses are preserved. Wilson and Soldal support the formal remedy. Joins Parts I–II. |
| Scalia | Affirm actual short processing; Robinette and Ayeni preserve independent execution and notice limits. | Unchanged. Paperwork/release serve this continuing offense; rejects local authority as unlimited constitutional permission. Dissents. |
| Kennedy | Affirm under Whren/Wilson/Robinette objective authority and execution limits. | Unchanged. Continuing violation and ordinary one-hour processing suffice without individualized impossibility of citation. Dissents. |
| Souter | Affirm under Robinette/Ayeni’s separate-intrusion inquiry. | Unchanged. This processing serves enforcement, unlike an unrelated private objective; state authority alone is insufficient. Dissents. |
| Thomas | Affirm under his Whren/Wilson opinions and Robinette join. | Unchanged. Actual limited processing supplies the additional connection; no fine-only categorical prohibition or waived warrant ground. Dissents. |
| Ginsburg | Vacate without deciding actual unreasonableness or damages; Robinette concurrence and Ayeni join. | Accepts targeted reversal of adverse custody judgment with application, causation and liability open; Wilson supports the remedy. Joins Parts I–II. |
| Breyer | Vacate for practical inquiry, retaining actual duration, processing and continuing-violation facts; Robinette/Ayeni joins. | Accepts targeted reversal with all supported facts retained, no automatic hearing and no least-restrictive-means duty; Wilson supports the form. Joins Parts I–II. |

The precise accommodation changes only the four original formal remedy labels from vacatur to targeted reversal while preserving their unchanged operative objective: remove the adverse custody judgment and adjudicate its application under the correct rule. Their reservations are essential; a present violation finding would exceed their commitments. Wilson demonstrates reversal of a deficient constitutional framework without deciding a violation; Soldal provides the analogous separation of adverse summary judgment from reasonableness/liability. No new §2106 interpretation is needed. The four affirmers’ application objections remain unanswered and their votes remain unchanged. These are supported circulation inferences, not recovered conversations.

Five now expressly support targeted reversal and remand; they share Part I’s actual rule, not Part II’s affirmative application reservation. Four regard application as open, Stone finds the custody unlawful, and four find it lawful. There is no majority application rule from these three positions and no logical-subset or Marks synthesis. The common judgment sets aside the categorical-ground custody judgment; lack of a Court finding of violation leaves ordinary application and liability proceedings without attributing that preference to Stone.

**Historical departure:** A reasoned merits disposition replaces the historical unexplained dismissal as improvidently granted, whose reason, tally and individual votes are unknown. Current Whren’s execution limits, Robinette’s later-restraint rule and Ayeni’s purpose-bound intrusion principle give Stevens, O'Connor, Ginsburg and Breyer specific grounds for rejecting the automatic formula while preserving application; Scalia, Kennedy, Souter and Thomas apply those same limits but find the short enforcement processing sufficient. No contrary individualized historical merits commitment or invented dismissal reason is attributed to any Justice. The limited formal-remedy revision creates no additional identifiable personal historical departure.

## Sources, cutoff and continuity

Research cutoff: May 4, 1998. The safe neutral packet, `../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK7_B_ADDITIONAL_NEUTRAL.md`, original reconciliation and circulation audit use the full Seventh Circuit opinion with all four footnotes and the official one-page historical order at 523 U.S. 613. The latter establishes only its public unexplained action and dates, not a poll or rationale. The petition, merits briefs, appendix and transcript are not represented as recovered.

The ordinance permits fines of $5–$500 per offense, each day a separate offense; no accumulated amount is adjudged. The continuing operation, accepted arrest authority, one-hour locked interview-room processing, documents and recognizance release are supported facts, not missing matters newly invented for remand. The wife’s license acquisition and charge dismissal do not themselves decide legality of the earlier restraint. Individual immunity was not adjudicated in the recovered opinion; absence of that account is not forfeiture.

Stone’s published separate position retains the actual-unreasonableness and narrower-remand conclusions. The four-Justice lead application position and four-Justice dissent retain their actual objective-enforcement disagreement for continuity. No damages, officer responsibility, immunity, new municipal policy or independent proceeding is created by this Record.

## Current-law refresh

The exact April 21–22 Public Projections in `../entering-law/OT_1997CHUNK7_B_CURRENT_PUBLIC.md` were screened before assembly. Atlantic Mutual’s reserve-transition construction, Beach’s specific rescission expiration and exception, and Campbell’s separate standing routes change no predicate here. Deep Sea Research concerns the unpossessed maritime res and its source-specific title/remedy inquiry; it supplies no general sovereign-immunity or remedial rule altering this case. Miller establishes the bounded permission to present the father’s claim but no controlling equality, citizenship-remedy or general reopening rule. Neither changes this case’s claimant, scope, governing doctrine or approved Stone position. Chaudhuri’s university-prayer/silence rule, Edwards’s bounded relevant-conduct rule, Calderon’s completed-habeas recall rule and Romani’s protected-property priority rule change no arrest-execution, municipal-liability or conduct-time-immunity predicate. Same-day Perry supplies no entering law.

## Assignment

**Form decided before counting:** One signed opinion announcing the judgment, with Part I an Opinion of the Court on the added-restraint rule and targeted reversal, and Part II a four-Justice explanation preserving the actual application for remand. Stone joins Part I and the reversal/remand judgment but separately concludes the custody was unreasonable and would confine remand to remaining liability and relief. The four affirmers dissent on the sufficiency of the actual enforcement connection. The genuine application difference determines the parts before any count; no Marks synthesis or division of lead authors is warranted because four Justices can carry the entire lead rationale.

**Assignment authority:** The Chief Justice is in the tentative judgment coalition and assigns. Agreement on the entire proposed rationale, rather than judgment alone, establishes eligibility.

| Justice | Count before assignment |
|---|---:|
| Stone-Zsela | 7 |
| Stevens | 9 |
| O'Connor | 8 |
| Scalia | 7 |
| Kennedy | 7 |
| Souter | 7 |
| Thomas | 7 |
| Ginsburg | 7 |
| Breyer | 7 |

**Last event counted:** Perry v. Los Angeles Police Department; Ninth Circuit No. 96-55545; no separate Supreme Court docket supplied.; 1998-05-04.

**Eligible authors:** Stevens, O'Connor, Ginsburg, Breyer.

**Balance pool:** O'Connor, Ginsburg, Breyer; eligible minimum 7, ceiling 8.

**Author selected:** Ginsburg. Fit chooses among the three pool members after the audited formal-remedy accommodation establishes the four full lead-opinion joins. Ginsburg Robinette concurrence preserves actual detention questions while accepting correction of an overbroad governing rule, precisely the distinction Part II must maintain here; her Ayeni join also keeps current constitutional limits and conduct-time liability distinct. Breyer offers equally practical record assessment, while the higher-count author of Robinette offers strong rule-construction capability. Ginsburg has the most direct published formulation for separating the common rule from the unresolved application and is at the eligible minimum. Stone assigns from the five-Justice judgment coalition but is not eligible for the entire lead opinion: his approved position decides actual unreasonableness and does not join its affirmative reservation. The four full joiners can carry both parts, so splitting lead authorship is unnecessary. The audited accommodation changes only the formal remedy label while retaining every application reservation; author identity changes no vote. Thomas writes the dissent through his Whren and Wilson execution analysis; the separate writing does not count.

The count was recomputed from actual current-term opinion tables immediately before writing this Record. Separates, per curiam, threshold, summary and other procedural actions do not count. Each signed plenary lead author counts once. Only the four formal-disposition revisions expressly supported by the frozen circulation audit occurred; all substantive application positions remain unchanged. No invented draft history supplies a join.

assignment_statements.text:
**Case and dockets:** Bousley v. United States, No. 96-8516.
**Event and date:** Merits decision; 1998-05-18 (OT1997, chunk 8).
**Result:** Reversed, 7–2; conditional gateway remand supported by six, with Stevens seeking immediate vacatur of the firearm conviction.
**Version / lineage:** Original decision.

## Posture, participation and entering law

Certiorari to the Eighth Circuit under §1254(1), after argument March 3, 1998. All nine Justices participate at argument and decision; quorum and a five-vote majority are available. This first §2255 proceeding is not a successive-authorization appeal. The drug conviction and sentence-quantity issue are outside this review. Research cutoff: May 18, 1998.

The entering-law slice supplies Bailey's active-employment meaning, Schlup's whole-record gateway, Carriger's separation of gateway and underlying constitutional claim, Godinez's separation of competence and informed choice, and Hyde's different presentence-withdrawal setting. Neither Plaut nor Morgan Stanley creates a criminal collateral exception. May 18 matters share the pre-group substantive baseline; alphabetical ordering governs assignments only.

## Frozen commitments, reconciliation and compatibility

Authoritative handoffs are the B preflight and commitments, the separately frozen Bousley preservation validation, and `../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK8_bousley_v_united_states_RECONCILED.md`. The original provisional handoff remains intact. Separate neutral and reconciliation contexts excluded Stone. Full historical Court, Stevens and Scalia writings and their notes were verified.

| Justice | Frozen reconciled ground and final position |
|---|---|
| Stevens | Reverses. Bailey and Rivers establish the substantive offense; Smith and Henderson protect real notice. Timmreck and Hill distinguish a formal Rule 11 defect from constitutional invalidity. He would vacate this firearm conviction and permit a new plea without default or innocence prerequisites. Joins Part I only; separately concurs in part and dissents in part. |
| O'Connor | Joins all parts. Bailey, Parke, Schlup and Hyde support the correct offense, informed assent and demanding factual gateway without automatic relief. |
| Scalia | Dissents. No cause excuses direct-review default; the trial-based Schlup gateway should not extend to guilty pleas with missing trial records, bargained exposure and stale proof. He does not equate possession with Bailey use. |
| Kennedy | Joins all parts. Broce separates antecedent claims from plea validity; McCleskey preserves default discipline; Bailey and Hyde retain their distinct roles. |
| Souter | Joins all parts. Schlup, Carriger and Godinez support actual whole-record examination, not an assumption that representation or capacity establishes informed assent. |
| Thomas | Joins Scalia's dissent on the same plea-specific gateway objection and no-cause ground. Godinez and Hyde do not decide this extension. |
| Ginsburg | Joins all parts. Lindh's provision-specific method and her Bailey, Schlup, Carriger and Hyde positions separate channel, offense, gateway and merits. |
| Breyer | Joins all parts. Bailey and the Schlup/Carriger inquiry permit the bounded whole-record opportunity while preserving real statutory and procedural limits. |

Reconciliation corrects unsupported provisional grounds on unchanged premises: Stevens did not merely reserve a forgone-charge point while accepting default; he rejects that prerequisite and seeks vacatur. Scalia and Thomas's sufficient objection concerns cause and extending the innocence gateway to pleas, rather than an independent holding that misinformation under former law necessarily produces an intelligent plea. No Justice-specific changed premise supported retaining those provisional discrepancies. No historical departure remains, and no historical author is imported.

Stone's approved `../runtime/OT_1997CHUNK8_bousley_v_united_states_STONE.md` requires reversal and remand through factual innocence, allows admissible evidence outside the plea record, forbids replacing the charged use offense with uncharged carrying, and leaves gateway and underlying entitlement to the district court. He joins Parts I–III and IV.B's application. The affirmative additional burden for an actually forgone more-serious offense in IV.A rests on the five Associates, rather than attributing a new general ground to Stone. His actual-case position is fully implemented; no fallback is used. There is no substantive refusal or invented drafting exchange to cure.

The five Associates join every part; Stevens joins the substantive/constitutional distinction in I but not II–IV's default, innocence burden or conditional mandate; Scalia and Thomas dissent. Stone's partial join is sufficient for the six-vote mandate. The five directly control IV.A without a Marks synthesis. Seven reject the Eighth Circuit judgment, but only six select this conditional remand. Stevens's stronger remedy remains visible.

## Assignment

Form first: one signed plenary lead opinion, with I addressing informed plea/substantive law, II default, III the factual gateway, IV.A actual forgone more-serious offenses and IV.B this indictment/remand. Separate writings preserve Stevens's distinct remedy and the Scalia/Thomas gateway objection. The parts follow legal differences before counting.

Chief Justice Stone-Zsela assigns from the conditional-remand coalition. Fresh actual-opinion-table counts immediately before assignment: Stone-Zsela 7; Stevens 9; O'Connor 9; Scalia 8; Kennedy 9; Souter 8; Thomas 7; Ginsburg 8; Breyer 8. Last counted event: Arkansas Educational Television Commission v. Forbes, May 18, 1998. Eligible complete-opinion authors: O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer. Minimum 8; pool includes all five at 8 or 9. Stone's partial rationale join does not qualify him for the entire opinion; no split authorship is needed because five can carry every part.

Ginsburg is selected for fit. Her Lindh opinion separates statutory channels and operative provisions, the central task in coordinating substantive innocence, default, plea validity and a limited mandate. O'Connor's Bailey authorship makes her a strong alternative, but Ginsburg can preserve that settled construction equally while carrying the distinct procedural stages and has the lower count. Souter and Breyer are equally counted alternatives; Ginsburg's provision-specific formulation supplies the concrete fit. No expansion accommodation or commitment change is invented.

## Sources and continuity

The neutral preservation supplement verifies only that the district court did not address actual innocence and that the Government did not contend waiver from failure to raise it below. The published explanation for the earlier omission is tentative, not a factual finding about Bousley's reason. This second preservation question is distinct from the unexcused failure to challenge plea intelligence on direct review. No original plea transcript or bargain agreement is claimed independently recovered; the published indictment and procedural recitations bound the decision.

Stevens's direct-vacatur rationale and Scalia/Thomas's plea-gateway objection remain noncontrolling positions. The decision orders an opportunity to establish the gateway, not acquittal, release or an automatic oral evidentiary hearing. All factual and constitutional issues identified below remain for lawful district-court proceedings. Vote arithmetic, partial joins, remedy and authority are consistent; final integration checks are recorded separately.

assignment_statements.text:
**Case and dockets:** Montana v. Crow Tribe of Indians, No. 96-1829.
**Event and date:** Merits decision; 1998-05-18 (OT1997, chunk 8).
**Result:** Reversed and remanded, 9–0; no automatic entitlement to the entire tax collection and no restitution amount fixed.
**Version / lineage:** Original decision.

## Event and governing record

Certiorari under §1254(1) to the Ninth Circuit's mandatory restitution direction, 92 F.3d 826. Argued January 14, 1998; decided May 18. All nine Justices participate at argument and decision; quorum and majority requirements are met. Research cutoff: May 18, 1998.

The entering-law slice and Montana refresh supply California, Fulton, Chickasaw Nation and the controlling prior invalidity of these taxes. The common pre-May-18 substantive baseline applies; same-date alphabetical order governs assignments only. Cotton Petroleum preserves the distinction between permissible concurrent taxation and this excessive state taxation. The prior invalidity judgment is neither reopened nor converted into a prohibition on every conceivable state tax.

The corrected objective facts matter to remedies. The United States intervened as trustee in June 1983. The 1988 ruling treated the original Interior reservation-tax approval as covering the ceded-strip minerals and the contrary exclusion as legally mistaken. The ruling distributed registry money under the 1982 agreement; it did not determine a pre-agreement Westmoreland debt. Actual approval disputes and the lessee's unwillingness to pay without approval permitting pass-through remain practical facts, not a dispositive absence of lawful tribal authority.

## Frozen commitments and historical reconciliation

Sources: original B preflight/commitments; MONTANA_OBJECTIVE_SUPPLEMENT; MONTANA_PREFLIGHT_REFRESH and MONTANA_COMMITMENTS_REFRESH; `../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK8_montana_v_crow_tribe_of_indians_RECONCILED.md`. The affected neutral review preceded the separately scoped reconciliation; neither saw Stone. All original handoffs remain intact. The complete historical Court opinion with seventeen notes and Souter's writing with its note were verified.

| Justice | Reconciled ground and final join |
|---|---|
| Stevens | Joins the bounded common opinion. Cotton Petroleum, his own opinion, distinguishes excess from complete state incapacity. Corrected approval coverage and the Tribe's resource interest do not establish entitlement to every receipt. |
| O'Connor | Joins the common reversal and express preservation of meaningful consideration of independent partial relief. Joins Souter's separate explanation; refuses a rationale effectively foreclosing the current partial claim through approval, agreement or taxpayer-refund barriers. |
| Scalia | Joins. California's claimant distinction and the actual arrangements defeat compulsory total transfer; he supports no mandatory award or reopening of proof. |
| Kennedy | Joins. Violation and entitlement to the particular remedy remain distinct; federal tribal interests and proper independent relief are preserved without a fixed amount. |
| Souter | Joins the narrow common opinion and separately explains the existing partial restitution theory. His full historical writing rejects the whole collection while allowing examination of all, some or none of its excessive share. |
| Thomas | Joins. California and Fulton's remedial distinctions supply no automatic assignment of another taxpayer's payments; no invented prior debt, tribal waiver or compensatory amount enters. |
| Ginsburg | Joins. Chickasaw's incidence principle is not a universal remedy; legal coverage, practical nonpayment and proven entitlement remain distinct. No compulsory additional recovery follows. |
| Breyer | Joins. Earlier trustee intervention and corrected coverage do not establish an amount or erase concurrent taxation; appropriate independent relief remains possible. |

Historical reconciliation corrected the refresh's Stevens/Souter/Breyer votes for affirming the entire award. The newly recovered approval and intervention facts were already present in the historical record. They were research corrections, not changed premises supporting departure. Souter's complete separate writing expressly rejected total disgorgement, and Stevens and Breyer joined reversal on those same facts. The actual California/Fulton/Chickasaw holdings supply no different total-entitlement rule. No historical judgment departure remains.

The all-nine opinion stops at the common ground and expressly leaves proper consideration of independent partial restitution open in this action. It does not adopt the additional reasoning that O'Connor and Souter oppose. Their affirmative trust-property restitution framework remains in their concurrence. The preserved difference is between a permissible lawful course on remand and their demand for meaningful adjudication of the existing lesser claim, not an established right to another dollar. This formulation is expressly within the reconciled shared draft; no commitment changes or invented circulation exchanges occur.

## Stone and assignment

Stone's approved `../runtime/OT_1997CHUNK8_montana_v_crow_tribe_of_indians_STONE.md` rejects automatic full restitution, preserves the invalidity ruling, separates the Tribe's entitlement from the taxpayer's position, and requires proper equitable analysis without fixing an amount. The opinion gives that position full effect. It considers payment, economic burden, agreements, waivers actually proved, prior distributions and duplicative recovery without presuming a tribal release or treating equity as a license to retain unlawful gains. No fallback is used.

Form first: one signed plenary opinion on the common distinction between invalidity and total recovery, and one concurrence stating Souter/O'Connor's additional partial-restitution rationale. Neither form nor scope depends on counts.

The Chief belongs to the judgment coalition and assigns. Fresh actual-table recount immediately before assignment: Stone-Zsela 7; Stevens 9; O'Connor 9; Scalia 8; Kennedy 9; Souter 8; Thomas 7; Ginsburg 9; Breyer 8. Last counted event: Bousley v. United States, May 18, 1998. All nine are eligible for the complete narrow opinion. Minimum 7; balance pool: Stone-Zsela, Scalia, Souter, Thomas and Breyer.

Stone-Zsela writes. His approved formulation directly supplies the opinion's necessary separation of unlawful collection, claimant entitlement and remedy, while expressly requiring examination rather than permitting a categorical no-relief shortcut. Souter is the strongest alternative because his condition identifies the existing partial claim that must remain genuinely open; Stone's formulation accommodates that condition without requiring the other Justices to adopt Souter's additional affirmative framework. Both can state the common rule, and Stone has the lower count. Thomas is equally counted and fully capable, but Stone's express treatment of taxpayer, fund, agreements and the anti-windfall/anti-retention limits supplies the case-specific advantage. This is fit and faithful scope coordination, not an authorship claim based on office or importance. Souter writes the concurrence joined by O'Connor.

## Continuity, source limits and validation

Severance receipts at issue cover 1975–1982, approximately $46.8 million; gross-proceeds receipts cover 1975–1987, approximately $11.4 million. Registry deposits began January 1983 and November 1987 respectively. These periods, the 1982 agreement, registry distributions and the taxpayer's separate refund position are not collapsed. The pleadings seek restitution and interest, not a proved compensatory-loss award. No decision permitting a proposed amendment or finding a new loss is supplied.

Souter/O'Connor's concurrence preserves an independent property-based partial-restitution approach, with all, some or none of the excessive share recoverable after proper analysis. It does not control the nine-Justice opinion's additional remedial method. Vote, joins, law/remedy distinctions and the limited mandate have been checked; all eleven Public Projection blocks follow. Final non-Git checks are separate.

**Case and dockets:** Ohio Forestry Association, Inc. v. Sierra Club; No. 97-16.
**Event and date:** Threshold decision after plenary argument; 1998-05-18; October Term 1997, chunk 8.
**Result:** Vacate and remand for dismissal without prejudice as unripe, 9–0; both lower merits adjudications are displaced.
**Version / lineage:** Original decision.

## Event, participation, and entering law

Argued February 25, 1998; decided May 18, 1998, the verified historical decisional date adopted for this event. Certiorari reviews the Sixth Circuit's judgment reversing summary judgment for the Forest Service and reaching the Wayne National Forest plan's substantive legality. The issue is whether the present substantive planning challenge is ripe before further site-specific authorization. The question is stated analytically, not as a quotation of a recovered petition.

All nine participate at argument and decision: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. No case-specific disqualification is established; quorum and the five-vote decision threshold are satisfied. Ripeness alone resolves the action. Standing, APA finality, NFMA and NEPA merits, public-trust duties and a distinct completed procedural claim are not decided.

The [entering-law slice](../entering-law/OT_1997CHUNK8.md) supplies Abbott Laboratories' fitness-and-hardship inquiry, the current March 31 Texas application, Bennett's consequential-agency-action rule, and Lujan's concrete-interest procedural protection. Toilet Goods distinguishes completed agency action from ripeness; New York and Pic-A-State preserve review of actual present burdens. These rules require examination of this plan's effects rather than an automatic delay whenever implementation discretion remains. The same-day cases supply no entering precedent. Research cutoff: May 18, 1998, immediately before this event.

## Stone's approved position and compatibility

The [approved supplement](../runtime/OT_1997CHUNK8_ohio_forestry_association_inc_v_sierra_club_STONE.md), researched reconstruction approved October 21, 2026, fixes vacatur/remand/dismissal without prejudice, ripeness-only resolution, no immediate logging authorization or present legal hardship, meaningful later project review, and preservation of independently binding provisions and properly presented completed procedural violations. Stone joins the entire bounded opinion below. No standing fallback, new alternative ground, substantive narrowing or separate writing is used.

The clean scope refresh identifies three legal theories within the substantive planning challenge, without establishing a new present injury or procedural deprivation. Accounting expressly for those theories implements the approved substantive-challenge disposition. The later motorized-use, road and trail assertions receive no independent adjudication; this preserves Stone's express nonreach. The current Texas and Bennett rules alter no controlled premise. Later review remains subject to its own requirements; the disposition does not promise relief or establish a future limitations or exhaustion rule.

## Judgment, opinion form, and assignment

All nine vote to vacate the Sixth Circuit judgment and remand for dismissal without prejudice as unripe. The District Court's substantive summary judgment must also be displaced. The disposition covers the NFMA/NEPA/APA plan and below-cost-clearcutting claim, the public-trust below-cost-sales claim, and the NFMA/APA timber-suitability-regulation claim. No merits judgment, plan invalidation, logging injunction, revision command or fee award is entered.

One signed opinion explains a reusable ripeness rule and the complaint-specific limits after plenary argument. Its form and propositions rest on this legal work. Scalia delivers it; all other Justices join in full. No separate writing performs additional legal work. 

The Chief assigns from the unanimous judgment coalition. Fresh actual-opinion-table counts immediately before assignment: Stone-Zsela 8; Stevens 9; O'Connor 9; Scalia 8; Kennedy 9; Souter 8; Thomas 7; Ginsburg 9; Breyer 8. Last counted event: Montana v. Crow Tribe of Indians, May 18, 1998. All nine are fully eligible. Minimum 7; balance pool: Stone-Zsela, Scalia, Souter, Thomas and Breyer. Scalia writes for fit: his Bennett opinion states why completed action with current effects may be reviewable despite remaining implementation, and his Lujan opinion preserves a concrete procedural interest. Those two limits are central to avoiding an overbroad wait-for-logging rule. Thomas has the lower count and is fully capable, but Scalia's direct formulation of both governing distinctions supplies the concrete advantage. Stone's approved practical-consequences formulation fits the common result, without an additional advantage over Scalia's coordinated authorities. No expansion accommodation or changed commitment is needed. This pure ripeness disposition is a threshold action, consistent with the term's Texas classification: assignment follows section 8, but this opinion receives no plenary-merits lead credit. The inventory's preparatory MERITS label does not turn the actual nonmerits dismissal into a merits adjudication.

## Frozen commitments and historical reconciliation

The [frozen reconciliation](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK8_ohio_forestry_association_inc_v_sierra_club_RECONCILED.md) retains the original [commitments](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK8_OHIO_COMMITMENTS.md) and [clean scope refresh](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK8_OHIO_COMMITMENTS_SCOPE_REFRESH.md). Every Associate supports the same judgment and every proposition below. The complete historical opinion corroborates the retained threshold result; historical authorship supplies no assignment. No historical departure is recorded.

| Justice | Individual sufficient ground and compatibility limit |
|---|---|
| Stevens | His current Texas opinion applies fitness and hardship to actual effects; Bennett and Pic-A-State preserve sufficiently consequential present review. All three substantive theories are premature here. He joins no assumed waiver of recreation assertions or unnecessary standing holding. |
| O'Connor | Her New York opinion permits review where future obligations require substantial current preparation. This record establishes no comparable burden. She joins with meaningful pre-cutting review and independent procedural claims preserved, without an injury-first or exhaustion rule. |
| Scalia | His Bennett and Lujan opinions distinguish consequential completed action and concrete procedural interests from an unproved timing premise. Finality and a NEPA label do not establish present injury. He joins without deciding statutory finality, trust merits or unidentified procedural claims. |
| Kennedy | His Pic-A-State opinion distinguishes a present conduct constraint from projected harvesting. His Bennett and Texas joins reject automatic postponement based on agency discretion. He requires neither injury before suit nor an invented waiver finding. |
| Souter | His Humane Society opinion and Bennett/Texas joins require a supported connection between challenged action and present consequence. The new recreation assertions supply no established connection in this reviewed dispute. He joins no categorical causation or preservation bar. |
| Thomas | His Lujan, Bennett and Texas joins support concrete consequences and threshold resolution before premature statutory adjudication. The regulation and trust claims must be included; he joins no unsupported procedural entitlement or forestry merits conclusion. |
| Ginsburg | Her Bennett, Texas and Humane Society joins distinguish present effects from future implementation. NEPA's pleaded role stays visible, but no denied procedure is identified. She joins only with environmental and recreational injury's possible cognizability intact. |
| Breyer | His Bennett and Texas joins support practical examination of consequences. General rules can constrain later choices, but neither that influence nor possible amendment alone decides ripeness. He joins the present-record rule, not an inflexible wait-for-implementation requirement. |

The strongest contrary path concerns a completed suitability regulation and alleged present recreation effects. Finality alone does not supply the missing current consequence; the later assertions are not established facts or an independently adjudicated earlier claim. The common formulation answers those concerns by addressing every substantive count, preserving independently consequential regulations and procedural injuries, and declining to decide the separate assertions. No vote changes or fictional circulation exchanges are claimed.

## Law, continuity, sources, and validation

The complete controlling holdings and their authority are stated in the Public Projection's Holdings block; its Precedent Treatment and Law After Decision blocks state their present force. All nine directly adopt them; no fractured-decision inference is necessary. The substantive legality of the plan remains open, and further agency projects retain their own notice, environmental-analysis and review requirements. No noncontrolling published position, new institutional practice, external follow-on event or dependent-case consequence is created.

The [clean packet](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK8_OHIO_NEUTRAL_CLEAN.md), [lower opinion](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK8_OHIO_LOWER_CLEAN.txt), [scope extraction](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK8_OHIO_NEUTRAL_SCOPE_SUPPLEMENT.md) and [fresh preflight](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK8_OHIO_PREFLIGHT_SCOPE_REFRESH.md) supply the material facts and boundaries. The lower decision is 105 F.3d 248. The published recitations in [523 U.S. 726–739](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-523/pdf/USREPORTS-523-726.pdf) support dates, plan operation, three pleaded theories, prayers for relief and later briefing. The original pleadings and full briefs are not claimed recovered. Under Engine §14 those recitations support this bounded disposition; an affirmative preservation finding about the new recreation theories would require the actual complaint and specific earlier submission. No research gap becomes litigant default. The historical Supreme Court writing is comparator evidence, not this Court's entering law.

assignment_statements.text:
**Case and dockets:** Stewart v. Martinez-Villareal; No. 97-300.
**Event and date:** Threshold decision after plenary argument; 1998-05-18; October Term 1997, chunk 8.
**Result:** Affirmed, 7–2; this previously presented and premature Ford claim returns for its first federal merits consideration. Ordinary review of the classification is available, 9–0.
**Version / lineage:** Original decision.

## Event, participation, and entering law

Argued February 25, 1998; decided May 18, 1998, the verified historical decisional date adopted for this event. Certiorari reviews the Ninth Circuit's judgment, 118 F.3d 628, holding authorization unnecessary and transferring the renewed claim to the District Court. The questions concern ordinary review under §§1254 and 2244(b)(3)(E), then whether this previously presented incompetency-to-be-executed claim falls within the second-or-successive mechanism. Neither competency nor the adequacy of Arizona's competency proceedings is before the Court for merits determination.

All nine participate at argument and decision: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. No case-specific disqualification is established; quorum and the five-vote threshold are satisfied. Three early federal applications ended for nonexhaustion. The March 1993 application actually included the Ford claim; the State obtained dismissal as premature. Relief granted on other grounds was reversed, with the 1996 mandate preserving later Ford litigation. After an unsuccessful early reopening request, an execution warrant and state competency proceedings, the District Court dismissed the renewed motion for lack of jurisdiction on May 16, 1997. The circuit's subsequent transfer was a ruling that authorization was unnecessary, not an authorization determination under the statutory permission criteria.

The [entering-law slice](../entering-law/OT_1997CHUNK8.md) supplies Felker's actual-authorization review bar, Triestman and Dorsainvil's enforcement of that channel, Calderon's distinction for a separate first-application judicial action, and the source-specific habeas rules in Lonchar, Lindh and Carriger. Calderon's completed-merits recall restriction does not itself classify a claim never adjudicated on the merits. Lindh and Carriger do not create an exemption from every AEDPA provision, and Lonchar cannot displace an applicable enacted bar. Ford's constitutional prohibition supplies the claim's subject, not a competency finding. All same-day cases share the pre-event baseline. Research cutoff: May 18, 1998, immediately before this event.

## Stone's approved position and compatibility

The [approved supplement](../runtime/OT_1997CHUNK8_stewart_v_martinez_villareal_STONE.md), researched reconstruction approved October 21, 2026, fixes affirmance, the actual circuit-return remedy, and meaningful first consideration of the claim earlier dismissed as premature. It forbids treating prematurity as a merits rejection, assuming incompetence, or granting automatic sentence relief. Its threshold expressly incorporates Section I's questions and posture, including the ordinary-review question.

Stone joins Parts I and II below. Distinguishing an actual authorization decision from the circuit's threshold classification gives effect to his approved reach and disposition; it supplies no broader collateral-review entitlement or alternative constitutional ground. The narrow previously-presented/premature classification directly implements his fixed reasoning. No standing fallback, unapproved narrowing, new hearing entitlement or separate writing is used. Current Calderon, Lindh and Carriger law changes no approved premise: this claim's federal merits remain unadjudicated, and the mandate supplies no general immunity from governing statutory conditions.

## Judgment, opinion form, and assignment

All nine support ordinary review of the circuit's classification. Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer affirm its return of this claim for district consideration. Scalia and Thomas would reverse and apply §2244(b)(1)'s dismissal command to the repeated claim. They do not propose discretionary authorization of a claim their rule requires dismissed.

A signed opinion after plenary argument states the review-channel holding in Part I and the particular claim's classification and remedy in Part II. All nine adopt Part I; the seven affirming Justices adopt Part II. One dissent by Scalia, joined by Thomas, preserves their shared application-based text and written-law objection. Its two connected grounds require no duplicate opinions merely because history contained two. Souter delivers the Court's opinion. 

The Chief assigns from the seven-Justice affirmance coalition. A fresh actual-table recount immediately before assignment gives Stone-Zsela 8; Stevens 9; O'Connor 9; Scalia 8; Kennedy 9; Souter 8; Thomas 7; Ginsburg 9; Breyer 8. Last counted event: Montana v. Crow Tribe of Indians, May 18, 1998. The subsequent Ohio Forestry threshold action supplies no lead-merits credit. Eligible authors for the entire opinion are Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer. Minimum 8; all seven are in the balance pool. Souter writes for fit: his Lindh, Lonchar and Carriger positions coordinate the particular application, the enacted provision and the opportunity for first review without converting that opportunity into a universal exception. His disagreement with Calderon's merits rule is expressly separated from the binding channel rule, allowing a precise account of what this case does and does not reopen. Ginsburg's Lindh authorship makes her the strongest alternative; Souter can carry the same provision-specific explanation and has the lower count. Stone's approved first-review distinction is fully shared, but adds no separate formulation needed to secure the joins; the case-specific statutory coordination favors Souter. No expansion revision or changed commitment is claimed. This is a threshold classification returning an unadjudicated claim for consideration, not a merits determination of that claim; consistent with the term's threshold-event classification it receives no signed lead-merits credit. The rule does not exclude a merits decision merely because it addresses procedural law.

## Frozen commitments, joins, and historical reconciliation

The [frozen reconciliation](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK8_stewart_v_martinez_villareal_RECONCILED.md) retains the Stewart section of the [B commitments](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK8_COMMITMENTS_B.md). The historical six/two Associate division corroborates the substantive commitments. Scalia and Thomas's present Part I joins rest on the frozen channel analysis and current Calderon rule; the historical Court opinion was not historically unanimous on its reasoning. Historical authorship and later orders supply no present assignment or Court action.

| Justice | Retained commitment and individualized basis | Final scope |
|---|---|---|
| Stevens | His Lonchar and Carriger opinions distinguish required first-application process and provision-specific restrictions; Schlup distinguishes actual merits treatment from filing count. A premature, expressly preserved claim remains unadjudicated. | Parts I–II; no universal later-claim exemption. |
| O'Connor | Her Felker opinion enforces the actual authorization bar; her Lonchar I–II and Carriger I joins preserve specified procedural predicates. The continuation classification requires no equitable exception or Lonchar III premise. | Parts I–II; otherwise applicable habeas rules remain. |
| Scalia | His Felker joins enforce the enacted repeated-claim rule. His reconciled written-law objection, supported by Bollman, rejects replacement of Congress's altered scheme with prior practice. The earlier application ended after merits adjudication of other claims. | Part I only; dissent from Part II, requiring repeated-claim dismissal. |
| Kennedy | His Felker and Calderon channel joins distinguish authorization from other judicial actions. His Lonchar position protects the opportunity actually due without automatic merits procedures. This is not reopening a completed Ford merits determination. | Parts I–II; no mandatory hearing or competency result. |
| Souter | His Lindh, Lonchar and Carriger joins call for provision-specific treatment. Counting a premature claim as exhausted review would defeat its first available adjudication. His Calderon dissent does not override that case's controlling rule. | Parts I–II; no general exemption for new later claims. |
| Thomas | His Felker and Lonchar joins require the actual written statute. Application finality, prior presentation and §2244(b)(1) control for him; a judicial reservation cannot add an exception after the first merits application ends. | Part I only; joins Scalia's dissent and its dismissal consequence. |
| Ginsburg | Her Lindh opinion identifies the actual application and particular provision. Her Lonchar/Carriger and Calderon-channel joins support this first consideration while refusing the circuit's categorical competency-only formulation. | Parts I–II at the previously-presented/premature scope. |
| Breyer | His Lonchar/Carriger positions support the legally required first opportunity; his Felker, Triestman and Dorsainvil joins preserve true channel restrictions. Procedural classification resolves this case without invalidating AEDPA. | Parts I–II; no categorical exemption or automatic relief. |

The principal objection is application-based finality: the earlier merits application ended, and this claim was presented in it. The seven-Justice opinion answers by treating the specifically premature claim's return as continuation, not by waiving or invalidating a conceded statutory restriction. That answer does not satisfy Scalia and Thomas, whose dissent remains. No other commitment or join changes; no fictional revision history is asserted. No material historical departure requires a new changed-premise line.

## Law, continuity, sources, and validation

The Public Projection's Holdings block states both complete controlling rules, each with its own authority; the unanimous channel proposition is distinct from the seven-Justice classification. No Marks analysis is needed. The circuit's district-return direction stands, and the competency claim proceeds under otherwise applicable law. No writ, stay, execution authorization, competence finding, approval of state procedure or mandatory new live hearing follows.

For continuity, Scalia's dissent, joined by Thomas, is a published noncontrolling position: after an initial merits application ends, §2244(b)(1) requires dismissal of a claim previously presented there despite its prematurity dismissal and a judicial reservation. A wholly unexhausted application dismissed without prejudice is different in their view. Their written-law objection rejects an exception resting only on prior judicial practice. They reach no competency merits or separate original-writ question. No other noncontrolling ground, new institutional practice or external follow-on event is admitted.

The Stewart portions of the [neutral packet](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK8_NEUTRAL_B.md), [objective supplement](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK8_B_OBJECTIVE_FACTS.md) and [preflight](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK8_PREFLIGHT_B.md) supply the bounded chronology. The complete [published report, 523 U.S. 637–652](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-523/pdf/USREPORTS-523-637.pdf), supports procedural recitations; the 1996 mandate is reported at 80 F.3d 1301, 1309 n.1. [AEDPA, Pub. L. 104-132](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-104publ132/html/PLAW-104publ132.htm), supplies the statutory amendment. The reconciliation read every historical writing and its notes; their content remains comparator evidence, not entering Court law. Original filings are not claimed independently recovered, and no missing filing becomes waiver or default. No new reconstructed event or timing premise is adopted.

Assembly validation: nine channel votes; seven affirmance votes and two dissents; seven full opinion adopters and two Part I joins; the dissent's statutory rule entails dismissal, not invented discretionary permission. The approved Stone position, reservations and district-return remedy match. Assignment was made after the preceding Record was durably written. Final non-Git integration validation is recorded separately; repository commit remains with the operator.

assignment_statements.text:
**Case and dockets:** Textron Lycoming Reciprocating Engine Division v. United Automobile Workers; No. 97-463.
**Event and date:** Threshold decision after plenary argument; 1998-05-18; October Term 1997, chunk 8.
**Result:** Reversed and remanded, 9–0; dismissal of the presented action for lack of the asserted §301(a) jurisdiction, without adjudicating fraud or independently supported claims.
**Version / lineage:** Original decision.

## Event, participation, and entering law

Argued February 23, 1998; decided May 18, 1998, the verified historical decisional date adopted for this event. Certiorari reviews the Third Circuit's judgment, 117 F.3d 119, reversing the District Court's jurisdictional dismissal. The granted question is whether LMRA §301(a), 29 U.S.C. §185(a), supplies jurisdiction over a union's action seeking damages for formation fraud and a declaration that its collective agreement is voidable without alleging either party's violation. The question is analytically stated, not quoted from an independently recovered petition.

The Union represented approximately 500 employees. The agreement, effective April 1, 1994 through April 1, 1997, prohibited strikes and required seven days' notice before subcontracting agreements. After Textron announced subcontracting plans affecting roughly half those jobs, the Union's November 1995 complaint alleged concealment of those plans during bargaining. It alleged no breach by either party and sought compensatory and punitive damages and a declaration of voidability. The reported record establishes no threatened strike or other actual threatened violation controversy. Alleged fraud is not found true; an asserted future enforcement controversy is not inferred from the requested declaration.

All nine participate at argument and decision: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. No case-specific disqualification is established; quorum and the five-vote threshold are satisfied. The actual statutory channel permits the Court to review the jurisdictional ruling. Fraud, breach, validity, an NLRA bargaining violation, general federal-common-law jurisdiction and state remedies remain unadjudicated.

The [entering-law slice](../entering-law/OT_1997CHUNK8.md) supplies Wooddell's member-beneficiary enforcement rule and Kokkonen's demand for an actual jurisdictional basis. Current Lexecon reinforces compliance with Congress's specified allocation rather than replacing it with practical preferences; it does not itself decide §301. The current Caterpillar–UAW Rule 46 dismissal supplies no labor merits rule. Same-day decisions supply no entering precedent. Research cutoff: May 18, 1998, immediately before this event.

## Stone's approved position and compatibility

The [approved supplement](../runtime/OT_1997CHUNK8_textron_lycoming_reciprocating_engine_division_v_united_automobile_workers_STONE.md), researched reconstruction approved October 21, 2026, fixes reversal and remand, the statutory suit-for-violation gateway, no standalone formation-fraud jurisdiction merely because a different plaintiff might later sue, and the availability of validity defenses within a genuine violation suit. It reserves fraud merits and requires independently supported claims to retain their own treatment.

Stone joins the entire opinion below. Preserving a genuine declaratory enforcement controversy does not manufacture one in this complaint: the holding relies on the actual absence of an alleged breach or established threatened violation. It does not decide that every anticipatory declaration falls within §301 or §1331. The opinion adds no broader proposition about nonfederal defenses to anticipated federal claims, no general common-law jurisdiction ruling, and no NLRB exclusivity ground. Those limits preserve his approved statutory-gateway rationale rather than narrow or replace it. No fallback, alternative merits ground or separate writing is used. Current entering law changes no controlled premise.

## Judgment, opinion form, and assignment

All nine reverse the Third Circuit and remand for dismissal of the presented action for lack of its asserted §301(a) jurisdiction. The remand does not decide fraud, contractual validity or liability. An independently available claim or jurisdictional theory must satisfy its own requirements; the unreviewed general-common-law theory is not decided here. No damages, injunction, strike permission, subcontracting authorization or Board remedy is ordered.

One signed opinion after plenary argument explains the statutory boundary and the necessary distinction between a standalone validity suit and a validity issue in genuine violation litigation. Its form and scope rest on those grounds. Thomas delivers it; all other Justices join in full. A separate writing is unnecessary because the adopted common formulation preserves every recorded qualification. 

The Chief assigns from the unanimous judgment coalition. Fresh actual-table recount immediately before assignment: Stone-Zsela 8; Stevens 9; O'Connor 9; Scalia 8; Kennedy 9; Souter 8; Thomas 7; Ginsburg 9; Breyer 8. Last counted event: Montana v. Crow Tribe of Indians, May 18, 1998; Ohio Forestry and Stewart are later threshold actions without lead-merits credit. All nine fully support every proposition and are eligible. Minimum 7; balance pool: Stone-Zsela, Scalia, Souter, Thomas and Breyer. Thomas writes for fit and balance. His frozen Kokkonen/Lexecon-based position keeps the enacted jurisdictional category distinct from questions that may be necessary within a qualifying suit. This opinion requires that exact distinction, with no categorical resolution of genuine declaratory controversies. Scalia's Kokkonen authorship is the strongest alternative, and Breyer's reservation defines a limit any author must preserve; both can write the common rule, as can Thomas, whose lower count favors this assignment once that complete fit is established. Stone's approved gateway formulation is equally achievable by Thomas, who has the lower count, so self-assignment offers no advantage. The shared omission of unnecessary declaratory doubts is already within every reconciled commitment; no new join or circulation history is invented. The actual disposition is jurisdictional before contract merits and receives no lead-merits credit, consistently with the term's procedural-event classifications.

## Frozen commitments, joins, and historical reconciliation

The [frozen reconciliation](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK8_textron_lycoming_reciprocating_engine_division_v_united_automobile_workers_RECONCILED.md) retains all eight Textron commitments in [commitments B](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK8_COMMITMENTS_B.md). Their common rule is complaint-specific. No Justice supports jurisdiction merely because the contract concerns federal labor law; none requires barring validity defenses or every genuine anticipatory enforcement dispute.

| Justice | Individual sufficient ground and exact join scope |
|---|---|
| Stevens | His Wooddell and Kokkonen joins distinguish enforcement of covered obligations from enlargement of the jurisdictional category; his Lexecon join preserves enacted limits. He joins the narrow statutory holding in full. His historical NLRB observation was additional, not a condition of the shared ground; no Board merits ruling is included. |
| O'Connor | Her Wooddell/Kokkonen and current Lexecon joins support applying Congress's category to the pleaded dispute. She joins in full with validity issues available when antecedent to a genuine violation controversy and no categorical declaratory prohibition. |
| Scalia | His Kokkonen opinion rejects jurisdiction enlarged by contract-related policy; Wooddell preserves the statutory dispute category despite admitting beneficiary plaintiffs. He joins the narrow text-and-necessary-issue rule. Broader declaratory questions were unnecessary even in his historical reasoning and remain undecided. |
| Kennedy | His current Lexecon opinion enforces the actual statutory grant and sequence; his Wooddell/Kokkonen joins support the same boundary. He joins all propositions without adding a rule about the unreviewed common-law theory. |
| Souter | His Wooddell/Kokkonen and Lexecon joins support uniform interpretation inside the authorized class, not extension to every validity dispute. He joins in full with ordinary defenses and genuinely supported declaratory enforcement controversies preserved. |
| Thomas | His Kokkonen and Lexecon joins support the enacted category. Wooddell controls without attributing to him participation there. He joins the full narrow opinion: contract existence and labor policy do not supply an allegation of violation. |
| Ginsburg | Her Kokkonen/Lexecon positions require an actual jurisdictional basis. She joins the complaint-specific dismissal, without converting the declaration's wording into an unpleaded enforcement threat or deciding independently lawful forums. |
| Breyer | His Lexecon join preserves statutory limits while his frozen reservation protects genuine prebreach declaratory adjudication. He joins the complete narrow opinion because it relies on the missing actual controversy and states no categorical contrary rule. |

The Union's strongest path invokes uniform federal labor law and decisions permitting validity defenses. Those premises explain why validity may be necessary to deciding an alleged violation; they do not turn every standalone formation-fraud action into such a suit. Conversely, a blanket ban on validity adjudication would defeat a court's ability to decide whether an enforceable contract was violated. The adopted distinction answers both concerns. No hypothetical strike, employer suit, breach or labor-board violation is supplied.

**Historical departure:** Breyer's full opinion join rests on a narrower formulation than the historical majority's discussion: this opinion omits the unnecessary doubts about reverse declaratory jurisdiction and preserves genuine enforcement controversies. His reconciled position and complete historical concurrence support the complaint-specific statutory ground, while withholding assent to those broader doubts. No judgment changes, and no broader proposition from his historical concurrence is attributed to the other Justices.

Stevens's historical additional concurrence likewise supplies no required present separate opinion; the reconciliation establishes his full agreement with the narrower sufficient ground. This compatibility assessment invents no draft exchanges, changes no frozen commitment and imports no historical author assignment.

## Law, continuity, sources, and validation

The Public Projection's Holdings block states the complete controlling rule and authority; its precedent and resulting-law blocks state the continued force of earlier decisions. All nine directly adopt the rule; no Marks inference is used. The underlying labor dispute and independently available routes remain for lawful proceedings. The Textron portions of the [neutral packet](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK8_NEUTRAL_B.md), [objective supplement](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK8_B_OBJECTIVE_FACTS.md) and [preflight](../freeze/OT_1997CHUNK8_PREFLIGHT_B.md) support the complaint and posture. Reconciliation separately read the complete Court opinion and both concurrences, including notes. Those writings support historical comparison, not new entering authority. Original briefs and appendix are not claimed independently recovered. The source account establishes allegations and the absence of an identified violation controversy, not the merits of concealment. No research limit becomes default, concession or waiver, and no reconstructed litigation event is adopted.

assignment_statements.text:
**Case and dockets:** Gavin v. Branstad; Eighth Circuit Nos. 96-3746 and 96-3748, 122 F.3d 1081; no separate Supreme Court docket supplied.
**Event and date:** Merits decision, 1998-05-21, October Term 1997, chunk 8.
**Result:** Affirmed and remanded, 9–0, for statutory adjudication; immediate termination rejected.
**Version / lineage:** Original decision.

## Event, jurisdiction, and participation

The authorized event follows full briefing; no Supreme Court oral-argument date is recorded. Section 1254(1) supports review of the Eighth Circuit judgment, reached through the certified §1292(b) appeal permitted to the State and United States. The lower chronology and unperformed preservation inquiry are detailed below.

All nine Justices named below participate at submission and decision. Quorum exists; five votes suffice. No recusal is established. Benjamin and Hadix are separate matters. Same-day Thompson supplies no entering law.

## Entering law and source scope

The May 7 final Benjamin public handoff, Rouse, and entering-law slice supply the governing current law. The November 26, 1997 amendment requires a current **and** ongoing violation in pending cases. Actual Morgan Stanley/Plaut displaces the lower opinion's historical finality account. Rufo remains distinct.

Research cutoff: immediately before May 21, 1998. The complete Eighth Circuit opinion, verified in preflight and reconciliation including its notes, supports the reported procedural facts. Original decrees, current reports, and underlying filings are not claimed recovered. Published recitations suffice under Engine §14; missing sources prove neither default nor compliance. No denied witness or hearing is inferred from Benjamin.

## Stone and final compatibility

The approved supplement supports affirmance/remand, independent statutory findings, and rejection of Article III, vested-future-enforcement and equality objections. Stone joins Holdings 1–3 and 5, bounded by Benjamin and the amended statute; no factual finding or unconditional termination is supplied.

The separately assumed independent-contract impairment objection is not expressly addressed by the supplement. The standing fallback supplies Stone's vote to reject that component and **no affirmative ground**. Stone therefore does not join Part IV, cannot author the whole lead opinion, and receives no attributed contract theory. This is the only fallback use. No approved choice is replaced or expanded.

## Adaptive audit annex

All eight reconciled commitments retain their judgment, grounds, and boundaries below. No circulation history or changed vote is invented.

| Justice | Individual ground and final join check |
|---|---|
| Stevens | Rouse/Benjamin full joins and actual Plaut majority join support changed-law adjudication. All parts joined: completed effects survive and no preservation finding is fabricated. |
| O'Connor | Rouse/Benjamin and Agostini joins distinguish prospective supervision. All parts joined: no universal hearing duty and no added Rufo prerequisite. |
| Scalia | Benjamin authorship, Rouse/Rufo joins, and Kokkonen distinguish judicial duties and independent agreements. All parts joined: neither contract relabeling nor missing original findings defeats preservation. |
| Kennedy | Rouse authorship and Benjamin full join support statutory, constitutional, and assumed-contract grounds. All parts joined: no finding against current injury or independent contractual rights. |
| Souter | Rouse/Benjamin, Rufo, and Plaut joins preserve judicial determination and historical effects. All parts joined: consent creates no immunity, but necessary corrective relief receives actual adjudication. |
| Thomas | Rouse/Benjamin and Agostini joins support enacted remedial conditions. All parts joined: no silence-based compliance finding, compulsory hearing, or extra equitable prerequisite. |
| Ginsburg | Rouse/Benjamin and Plaut joins require genuine current-law adjudication. All parts joined: absent original findings do not mean absent present violations or automatic contractual survival. |
| Breyer | Rouse/Benjamin and Plaut joins support remedy-specific evaluation. All parts joined: neither continuation nor termination rests on abstract preferences. |

No historical Supreme Court merits lineup exists. The lower result agrees, but its original conjunction and historical Plaut rationale do not govern. Reconciliation finds no changed commitment, historical Supreme Court departure, or later-case consequence.

Immediate termination omits §3626(b)(3); permanent decree immunity conflicts with prospective-remedy law. The unanimous judgment has nine rationale votes in Parts I–III and V, eight in Part IV. Direct majorities control; no Marks synthesis applies.

## Opinion form and assignment

Signed lead opinion in five parts, selected before counting because this separately reviewed constitutional judgment requires explanation of amended statutory operation, distinct constitutional grounds, and a bounded remand. One Associate Justice can carry every part. No separate writing is necessary. Chief Justice Stone-Zsela assigns from the judgment coalition; eligibility for the whole lead opinion is confined to the eight Associates because Stone lacks an approved Part IV rationale.

Fresh actual-opinion-table recount immediately before assignment: Stone-Zsela 8; Stevens 9; O'Connor 9; Scalia 8; Kennedy 9; Souter 8; Thomas 7; Ginsburg 9; Breyer 8. Last counted event: Montana v. Crow Tribe of Indians, May 18, 1998; the subsequent Ohio Forestry, Stewart and Textron threshold actions carry no lead-merits credit. All eight Associates are eligible for the complete opinion; Stone's fallback vote on the assumed-contract component gives him no full-opinion eligibility. Minimum 7; balance pool: Scalia, Souter, Thomas and Breyer. Scalia writes for fit and coordination. His May 7 Benjamin opinion supplies the governing amended conditions and constitutional analysis, while identifying the different evidentiary problem there. The work here is to apply those rules to an unperformed statutory inquiry without importing Benjamin's actual refusal-of-proof finding. That direct coordination gives Scalia an advantage over the fully capable Thomas at the lower count. Souter's Rufo position supplies another strong alternative, but Rufo's separate equitable route is already settled and is not this case's disputed source of additional conditions. All necessary joins are within the frozen shared grounds; no expansion negotiation, changed vote or fictional revision is claimed. The signed plenary merits opinion receives one lead-author credit for Scalia.

## Continuity and validation status

The holdings below supply the complete controlling-holding section and Public Projection, applying amended termination doctrine without overruling precedent. Remand has no predetermined findings, release, deadline, or automatic return. No new noncontrolling position, roster change, or institutional practice results.
