**Case and dockets:** United States v. Thompson; CAAF No. 96-1412-AF, CCA 31803, 47 M.J. 378; no separate Supreme Court docket supplied.
**Event and date:** Merits decision, 1998-05-21, October Term 1997, chunk 8.
**Result:** Affirmed on both reviewed questions, 9–0; convictions and sentence remain undisturbed.
**Version / lineage:** Original decision.

## Event, jurisdiction, and participation

The authorized merits event follows full briefing, with no supplied Supreme Court oral-argument date. May 21, 1998 is the scheduling premise rather than a historical Supreme Court decision date. Section 1259 review rests on CAAF's actual grant of the marital-privacy issue and specification of the closed-session issue, verified by the complete issuing-court opinion. The Court reviews CAAF's December 16, 1997 judgment affirming the Air Force Court of Criminal Appeals. It does not infer jurisdiction from a mere refusal to grant review.

All nine Justices participate at submission and decision: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer. No recusal is established. Quorum exists and five votes suffice. The separate same-day Gavin event supplies no entering law; their processing order creates no dependency.

## Entering law and source-to-fact map

The frozen neutral preflight repairs the packet's original unavailable-source lead with the complete issuing-court opinion at `research/lower/thompson_caaf.txt`. That text establishes the granted and specified issues, convictions under Articles 128(a), 128(b), and 125, approved sentence, armed assault, Article 39(b) violation, verbatim transcript furnished at trial, completed findings, administrative questions, and answers unobjectionable in open session. CAAF's report, not a claimed independently recovered transcript, supports the bounded record inquiry under Engine §14. No party default, missing defense filing, or adverse inference arises from the research limits.

The sentence was a bad-conduct discharge, thirty months' confinement, total forfeitures, and reduction to the lowest enlisted grade. No distinct sentencing error is presented. The unpublished lower military decision, original merits briefs, and transcript itself are not claimed independently read. The reported source supplies the relevant findings without manufactured testimony or supplementation.

Research cutoff: immediately before May 21, 1998. Entering law includes the relevant autonomy holdings, Weiss, Sullivan, Rushen/Gagnon, and the March 31 public Scheffer decision. Richenberg's military-service question and Scheffer's evidence rule do not create general constitutional immunity. The asserted intimacy premise is considered without adopting a new categorical Article 125 rule. Article 59(a) and Allbee place the rebuttal burden on the Government for this Article 39(b) error.

## Stone and supported scope

The approved supplement expressly supports both affirmances. On privacy, Stone distinguishes an act undertaken to divert an ongoing deadly assault from voluntary intimacy; he reserves genuinely voluntary private conduct between spouses or other adults. On procedure, he recognizes the violation and permits the complete ministerial record to rebut prejudice where findings were already reached and the exchange was fully disclosed. His references to a complete record are fulfilled by the supported published recitation, without claiming retrieval of the original transcript.

Stone joins both controlling propositions and their precise limits. The Government's burden is inherited law, not an added defense obligation. No fallback applies, no approved choice is replaced, and no extra constitutional or military exception is attributed to Stone. The assignment below implements that complete shared scope.

## Adaptive audit annex

All eight reconciled commitments support both judgment components on the same bounded grounds. The following final compatibility checks preserve each individual limit without inventing negotiations or changing a vote.

| Justice | Individual support and join boundary |
|---|---|
| Stevens | His Casey autonomy position concerns voluntary choice; Weiss's contextual safeguards and his Sullivan join distinguish this assessable contact from loss of a valid verdict. Joins both holdings without a marital-benefit test or military exemption. |
| O'Connor | Her Casey position, Weiss contextual join, and Sullivan join support the choice and assessable-error distinctions. Joins both: physical initiation proves no free consent, and defense silence cannot shift the Government's burden. |
| Scalia | The invoked Griswold premise does not reach this coercive setting; his Weiss historical ground preserves enacted safeguards, while his Sullivan opinion identifies the different absent-verdict defect. Joins the confined grounds, not a new consensual-conduct rule. |
| Kennedy | His Casey position, Weiss opinion, and Sullivan join preserve voluntary choice, independent military scrutiny, and the valid-verdict distinction. Joins both without treating every judge-member communication as harmless. |
| Souter | Casey/Weiss contextual joins and Sullivan support real autonomy and safeguards. Joins both because the report establishes already-completed findings; appellate review cannot supply unresolved merits findings. |
| Thomas | His Weiss historical concurrence and Sullivan join preserve Articles 39 and 59 while distinguishing structural error. Joins the failed voluntary-intimacy premise without broader marital-liberty or military-exemption conclusions. |
| Ginsburg | Her Weiss contextual join requires actual protections, and binding autonomy law concerns voluntary choice. Joins both without the lower court's broad marital-benefit formulation; Government rebuttal must rest on the reported communication. |
| Breyer | His public Scheffer position retains adjudicative scrutiny within military rules; autonomy law and Rushen/Gagnon permit these bounded grounds. Joins without extending evidentiary discretion into ex parte authority, waiver, or an absent-source presumption. |

The strongest privacy alternative rests on marriage and physical initiation; the proved assault defeats the voluntary-choice premise without resolving genuinely consensual conduct. The strongest procedural alternative stresses judicial influence before announcement and inability to participate. The affirmative reported exchange answers that danger here: completed findings, worksheet-only questions, no substantive instructions, complete recording, and disclosure at trial. Lack of an identified challenge or clarification corroborates that account and is not its substitute.

Historical reconciliation verifies the complete CAAF per curiam affirmance and absence of a separate writing. There is no historical Supreme Court lineup from which to depart. The Court adopts a narrower privacy basis than the lower court's general marital-benefit suggestion and does not enlarge its nonconstitutional classification into a rule for all contacts. No materially changed premise, new commitment, or renewed reconciliation is required. No historical-departure or downstream-consequence label is warranted.

## Opinion form and assignment

One signed lead opinion with two holdings is appropriate before any counts: the plenary review resolves distinct constitutional and statutory questions through shared, bounded reasoning. No separate writing or split authorship is needed. All nine join each holding and the entire judgment; each is eligible on substantive grounds. Stone assigns as Chief from the judgment coalition. Direct majority authority controls, with no Marks aggregation.

Fresh actual-opinion-table recount immediately before assignment: Stone-Zsela 8; Stevens 9; O'Connor 9; Scalia 9; Kennedy 9; Souter 8; Thomas 7; Ginsburg 9; Breyer 8. Last counted event: Gavin v. Branstad, May 21, 1998, preceding this independent peer alphabetically. All nine are eligible for the complete opinion. Minimum 7; balance pool: Stone-Zsela, Souter, Thomas and Breyer. Thomas writes for fit and balance. His Weiss concurrence keeps the military system's enacted protections operative, and his Sullivan join distinguishes an assessable recorded violation from the absence of a valid verdict. Those premises carry the statutory holding without replacing the Government's burden with defense silence. His frozen privacy position rests only on the missing voluntary-intimacy premise, allowing the narrow assault holding without resolving consensual conduct. Souter's contextual Weiss/Casey positions are a strong alternative and support the same two limits; both can express the complete shared rule, and Thomas has the lower count. Stone's approved two-part formulation is likewise faithfully achievable by Thomas at the lower count, so self-assignment adds no coalition or scope advantage. No expansion accommodation, new join, hypothetical constitutional ruling or invented circulation history is used. This signed plenary merits opinion receives one lead-author credit for Thomas.

## Continuity and validation status

The holdings in the Public Projection constitute the complete controlling-holding section. The conviction and approved sentence remain in force without remand, evidentiary hearing, release, or further prescribed Supreme Court proceedings. No new noncontrolling position, institutional practice, roster change, or broader Article 125 answer is created.
